Wheeler, Mohamed Trebak, Nicholas K.H. Khoo, Oren Rom, Fei Chang, Francisco J. Schopfer

10.1126/sciadv.aef1693.title: CREBBP loss drives immune evasion by epigenetically silencing STING and MHC-I in small cell lung cancer
10.1126/sciadv.aef1693.abstract: Most small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) exhibit low immunogenicity and intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify CREBBP loss, a frequent genetic alteration in SCLC, as a key suppressor of tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses that drives an immune-cold tumor microenvironment in Rb1/Trp53 -driven autochthonous mouse models. Consistently, Crebbp deletion promotes immune escape in syngeneic SCLC models. Mechanistically, Crebbp loss suppresses Sting and major histocompatibility complex class-I expression by reducing histone H3 acetylation. Notably, HDAC inhibition restores histone acetylation, reactivates these silenced genes, and induces tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses. Moreover, pharmacological HDAC inhibition synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade to suppress tumor growth in both Crebbp -mutant and Crebbp -wild-type SCLCs, with a more prominent effect in Crebbp -mutant tumors. Collectively, these findings establish CREBBP loss as a key mechanism of immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in SCLC, highlighting HDAC inhibition as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.
authors: Qing Gao, Kehong Wei, Deshen Pan, Chaoliang Xu, Yufei Xi, Yan Zhang, Arnaud Augert, David MacPherson, Deshui Jia

10.1126/sciadv.aeh9320.title: In-memory phononic learning toward cognitive mechanical intelligence
10.1126/sciadv.aeh9320.abstract: Mechanical intelligence seeks autonomous materials that embody memory, perception, learning, and decision-making within the mechanical domain. A fundamental challenge is to integrate memory with information processing in an efficient, scalable, and interpretable way that supports cognitive learning and decision-making. Here, we introduce in-memory phononic learning, a framework that unifies non-volatile mechanical memory with wave-based perception in a phononic metastructure. Spatial information is stored as structural states that program elastic-wave responses, allowing probing waves to act as queries that retrieve informative features through parallel, physically transparent localization modes. Learning is achieved by offline optimization of input waveforms to selectively combine these features for multitask memory-pattern recognition without hardware redesign, with decisions inferred directly from output-energy responses. We experimentally and numerically demonstrate high-accuracy classification across tasks from geometric shapes to handwritten digits. Overall, this work elevates “materials that compute” toward “cognitive matter” that can interpret, reason, and learn through wave physics, laying a foundation for scalable and robust autonomous material systems.
authors: Yuning Zhang and K. W. Wang

10.1126/sciadv.aeg7646.title: Chemically encoded pH-tunable covalent adhesion by a bacterial thioester domain
10.1126/sciadv.aeg7646.abstract: Thioester domains (TEDs) represent a family of bacterial adhesin domains that mediate covalent anchoring to target ligands via an intramolecular thioester bond. Although the broad distribution of TEDs among Gram-positive bacteria suggests a critical functional role, the biological significance of this covalent mechanism remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that TED-mediated covalent anchoring is reversible and that its equilibrium is regulated by pH. Specifically, SfbI-TED from group A Streptococcus binds tightly to fibrinogen at physiological pH, whereas mild acidification to pH 6.0 induces rapid dissociation of the complex. Thermodynamic analyses indicated that this pH responsiveness is largely dictated by the intrinsic pH sensitivity of the thioester-mediated acyl transfer reaction conserved within TEDs, rather than by surface residues specific to individual TEDs. Similar pH-dependent behavior was observed in phylogenetically distinct TEDs, suggesting that pH-responsive adhesion is likely to be a broadly shared feature of TED-containing adhesins across Gram-positive bacteria.
authors: Yuki Tokunaga, Ryo Matsunaga, Hiroko Kozuka-Hata, Masaaki Oyama, Kouhei Tsumoto

10.1126/sciadv.aec7416.title: In situ processing of fibrous hydrogels by photochemistry for adaptive cellular microenvironments
10.1126/sciadv.aec7416.abstract: Omnipresent in biology, fibrous networks like collagen possess unique properties: dynamic network via crosslinking and degradation. This intrinsic adaptivity plays a critical role in regulating cell behavior via cell-matrix interactions. Built from biological building blocks, however, these networks are challenging to manipulate or even control. Here, we introduce dynamic network regulation via photochemical control in a synthetic and fibrous highly biomimetic hydrogel. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that the dynamic control over the mechanical properties of this adaptive in vitro model can be used to modulate cell spreading and mechanotransduction in three-dimensional (3D) mesenchymal stromal cell cultures. Our approach not only opens the door to on-demand mechanically adaptive gels with unprecedented control, but simultaneously offers easy processibility and cell extraction of the used synthetic gel.
authors: Wen Chen, Zhengdong Gao, Hongjuan Weng, Hongbo Yuan, Roy van Alst, Rong Wang, Jyoti Kumari, Lorenzo Moroni, Paul H. J. Kouwer

10.1126/sciadv.aed2741.title: Single-cell-level digital twins for preterm birth prevention strategies
10.1126/sciadv.aed2741.abstract: Digital twin models can accelerate therapeutic development by enabling low-risk testing of candidate interventions. In preterm labor (PTL), a major pregnancy complication where clinical trials face ethical and financial barriers, digital twins are especially valuable for evaluating new therapies targeting immune dysfunctions driving PTL. Yet, current models lack single-cell resolution, limiting detection of cell type-specific mechanisms, off-target effects, and the design of personalized interventions. We present Simulated Immunome Modeling of Clinical Outcomes (SIMCO), a single-cell-level digital twin framework that models immunomodulatory treatment effects on the timing of labor using immunome-wide, single-cell simulations. SIMCO’s digital twins are trained and validated on a newly generated mass cytometry atlas of the pregnant immunome exposed to nine candidate drugs preselected for PTL prevention. Applying SIMCO to an independent cohort of pregnant individuals, we simulate treatment effects on gestational length, screening for candidate drugs that delay labor timing and providing system-level mechanistic insight for each drug candidate. Tetrahydrofolate and the combination of aspirin and lansoprazole emerged as top candidates for PTL prevention, delaying labor onset primarily through enhanced mTOR signaling in innate immune cells and attenuated JAK/STAT signaling in naïve CD4 + T cells.

10.1126/sciadv.aeh5819.title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia
10.1126/sciadv.aeh5819.abstract: Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.
authors: Hsi T. Wei, Dominic Boutet, Rukun Dou, Jessica Ahrens, Nadia Zeramdini, Alban Voppel, Fernando Gonzales-Aste, Fatme Abboud, Sylvain Baillet, Lena Palaniyappan

10.1126/sciadv.aeg2217.title: Climatic niche conservatism shapes the macroevolution, extinction, and survivorship of crocodile-line archosaurs
10.1126/sciadv.aeg2217.abstract: Crocodylians are iconic thermophiles. Over 250 million years, crocodile-line archosaurs endured hyperthermals, climatic and range shifts, and two mass extinctions. Whether this niche conservatism reflects a deep evolutionary constraint or recent adaptation to novel climates remains unclear. We integrate present-day occurrences with a time-scaled phylogeny of >400 fossil and extant species. Niche models calibrated on living crocodylians were projected across 245 million years and compared with paleophylogeographic reconstructions. Macroevolutionary model fitting shows that temperature and precipitation exhibit strong phylogenetic structure, best described by bounded Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics, indicating long-term niche conservatism. Poleward expansions in warm intervals and contractions in cool phases reflect tracking of conserved optima rather than niche evolution. Unlike non-avian dinosaurs, low-latitude suitability persisted across all but the most extreme end-Cretaceous scenarios, with recovery expanding from tropical refugia. Thermal and precipitation regimes shifted near the Cenomanian/Turonian hyperthermal (∼93.9 Ma) and Eocene/Oligocene aridification transition (∼33.9 Ma), respectively. Climatic niche conservatism is therefore ancient in crocodile-line archosaurs, but not completely static.
authors: Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, Alexandra F. C. Howard, Grace L. Varnham, Alex Farnsworth, Paul J. Valdes, Philip D. Mannion

10.1126/sciadv.aei4751.title: Wave vortices around oscillating subwavelength holes: Water-wave observation
10.1126/sciadv.aei4751.abstract: We consider a two-dimensional wave system containing a subwavelength hole, such as an aperture in an interface supporting surface electromagnetic or acoustic waves or an island in a fluid surface sustaining gravity-capillary waves. Recent studies have revealed the emergence of pronounced wave vortices around such structures, termed type II vortices, in contrast to conventional (type I) vortices associated with phase singularities and intensity nulls. A notable natural manifestation of type II vortices occurs in ocean tides around islands such as New Zealand, Madagascar, and Iceland, where the tidal phase increases by ±2π around the island. Although this phenomenon is usually associated with the Coriolis effect from the rotation of the Earth, here, we demonstrate the controlled generation of type II vortices using a minimal and tunable setup: a dipole-oscillating subwavelength hole and a single incident plane wave. Using laboratory gravity-capillary waves and an oscillating subwavelength “island,” we directly measure the resulting phase structure, topological charge, and wave angular momentum. We show that the emergence and handedness of the vortices can be precisely controlled via the relative phase between the dipolar source and the incident wave. Our results offer a simple and versatile mechanism for engineering subwavelength wave vortices, with potential applications in a variety of two-dimensional wave systems.
authors: Junyi Ye, Zheyi Li, Alexey Y. Nikitin, Franco Nori, Wenzhe Liu, Konstantin Y. Bliokh, Lei Shi

10.1126/sciadv.aen0211.title: Building digital pregnancies from the single cell up
10.1126/sciadv.aen0211.abstract: Single-cell digital twins connect in vitro drug screening studies with clinical outcomes, providing a new framework to evaluate therapies and advance precision medicine in pregnancy.

10.1126/sciadv.aeg6983.title: Ultrafast RIXS of orbital-resolved valence-band reshaping in photoexcited graphite
10.1126/sciadv.aeg6983.abstract: Ultrafast photoexcitation can drive solids far from equilibrium by dynamically renormalizing their electronic structure, yet direct time-domain access to bulk band-structure reshaping with orbital and momentum selectivity has remained limited. Here, we show in photoexcited graphite that femtosecond carbon K -edge resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS), used in the time domain, provides a momentum- and orbital-selective spectroscopic fingerprint of transient valence-band reshaping. Momentum- and orbital-selective measurements along the K → M contour disentangle π and σ contributions and reveal a structured redistribution of spectral weight emerging within ∼70 femtoseconds and evolving on picosecond timescales. Nonequilibrium first-principles RIXS calculations performed within a frozen-lattice approximation show that the earliest response is dominated by electronic correlations and transient screening. At longer delays, the dynamics become strongly momentum dependent: Near K , the signal reflects the decay of the electronic contribution to the renormalized band structure under a hot-phonon bottleneck, whereas at the M -point van Hove singularity, it reveals a characteristic spectroscopic signature consistent with electron-phonon-driven band red shift and lifetime broadening induced by strongly coupled optical phonons. A three-temperature model constrained by the orbital-resolved tr-RIXS data captures the ensuing energy cascade through a hot-phonon reservoir dominated by the E 2 g and A 1 ′ modes. These results establish time-domain RIXS as a complementary probe of transient band-structure renormalization and mode-selective energy flow in quantum materials.

10.1126/sciadv.aee2305.title: Prediction of mild cognitive impairment progression using time-sensitive multimodal biomarkers
10.1126/sciadv.aee2305.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) develops silently for years before symptoms emerge, making early identification of at-risk individuals essential for prevention trials and early intervention. We tested whether combining neurophysiological, imaging, and blood biomarkers improves prediction of progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in cognitively unimpaired older adults with a family history of AD ( n = 102; 31 progressors; mean follow-up of 5.9 years). Magnetoencephalography, magnetic resonance imaging, plasma biomarkers, and amyloid and tau positron emission tomography each captured complementary aspects of disease biology. Multimodal models predicted progression more accurately than demographic and genetic factors alone. Higher MEG alpha power was associated with increased near-term risk, whereas higher gamma activity predicted lower near-term risk; both effects weakened over time. Higher neocortical amyloid burden predicted increasing risk over follow-up, whereas plasma biomarkers and entorhinal tau predicted higher risk without significant time-varying effects. These findings support a time-sensitive multimodal framework for identifying cognitively unimpaired individuals at risk of MCI due to AD.

10.1126/sciadv.aeg5294.title: AMPK phosphorylation proceeds through hierarchical proteoform cascades revealed by integrated mass spectrometry
10.1126/sciadv.aeg5294.abstract: Protein kinases integrate cellular signals through complex phosphorylation cascades, yet resolving how chemical perturbations trigger and modulate these cascades in therapeutic targets remains a major challenge. Here, we dissect adenosine 5′-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) proteoforms during activation through controlled biochemical reactions with a hybrid mass spectrometry (MS) approach integrating bottom-up MS for site-specific kinetics with top-down proteoform characterization. We reveal that AMPK phosphorylation proceeds through hierarchical cascades rather than binary switching, with dual entry points: canonical calcium- and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase kinase 2 (CaMKK2)-mediated phosphorylation or allosteric activator PF-739 both triggering extensive autophosphorylation with α1-Ser496 (S496) showing the highest kinetic priority. Proteoform-resolved analysis uncovers channeled β1-Ser24/25 (S24/25) + Ser108 (S108) cophosphorylation linking subcellular localization with allosteric responsiveness. Site-directed mutagenesis demonstrates CaMKK2 targets only α1-Thr183 (T183), with all other modifications arising through autophosphorylation. Phosphatase competition reveals asymmetric control where PP1A selectively removes activation-loop phosphorylation while autophosphorylation sites remain protected, establishing persistent regulatory states. Resolving AMPK’s temporal kinetics and proteoform architecture during activation enables a proteoform-centric understanding on kinase regulation.

10.1126/sciadv.aef7693.title: Molecular-driven lead-free halide photoferroelectric solid solution for high-temperature sensitive self-powered x-ray detection
10.1126/sciadv.aef7693.abstract: Halide double perovskite ferroelectrics have recently emerged as an environmentally friendly candidate in radiation detection, photovoltaics, and optoelectronic memory devices due to their unique spontaneous polarization and semiconductor properties. However, it is a huge challenge to achieve efficient carrier transport and high Curie temperature ( T c ) in double perovskite ferroelectrics, owing to the limitations of twisted frameworks and structural construction. Here, we present a high- T c heterovalent metal solid solution double perovskite ferroelectric, (4Br2FBZ) 2 CsAgBiBr 7 (4Br2FBZ-CAB, 4Br2FBZ = 4-bromo-2-fluorobenzylammonium), through a strategy of cation-engineered symmetry regulation. The metal ions Ag and Bi transitioned from an alternating arrangement to a mixed-site solid solution pattern, effectively optimizing the electronic band structure to enhance carrier transport. Meanwhile, 4Br2FBZ-CAB exhibits a high T c of 484 kelvin, substantially expanding the family of high- T c lead-free ferroelectrics. Benefiting from its remarkable photoelectric and ferroelectric properties, a high self-powered x-ray detection sensitivity of 273.8 microcoulomb per gray per square centimeter (μC Gy air −1 cm −2 ) was achieved at room temperature. In addition, this exceptionally high T c enables the detector to operate self-powered at high temperatures, resulting in an excellent sensitivity of 896.9 μC Gy air −1 cm −2 and a low detection limit of 13.9 nGy air s −1 at 425 kelvin. This work opens an avenue for expanding the family of high- T c lead-free perovskite ferroelectrics with superior semiconducting properties.

10.1126/sciadv.aej0610.title: A pro-natural product design strategy affords ester-based green fungicide candidates
10.1126/sciadv.aej0610.abstract: Natural products (NPs) serve as both inspirations and resources for the discovery of bioactive compounds. However, their application in green agrochemical discovery faces limitations such as low activity, short duration of efficacy, potential toxicity and residue issues from structural modifications, and constraints in exploring chemical and biological space. Here, we propose the concept and design principles of pro-natural products (PrNPs), which effectively address these limitations and open a broad avenue for bioactive compound discovery. PrNPs are functional compounds designed to degrade into NPs under application conditions. Using this strategy, we designed and synthesized a structurally diverse ester-based PrNP collection with 170 members by combining natural acids and alcohols and found a promising green fungicide candidate, PrNP 6E , with excellent control efficacy against major plant diseases such as rapeseed Sclerotinia stem rot, rice sheath blight, and apple Valsa canker. Cheminformatic analysis, antifungal activity, degradation behavior, and safety assessment reveal that 6E combines the advantageous properties of both NPs and agrochemicals and exhibits suitable duration of efficacy, controllable degradation into NPs after fulfilling its function, broad safety, and environmental compatibility. The PrNP strategy shows great potential in enhancing the efficiency of finding green agrochemicals with novel chemotypes and mechanisms of action and in promoting sustainable development of agriculture.

10.1126/sciadv.aec8647.title: Dams trigger long-term river-floodplain decoupling in dynamic Andean foreland rivers
10.1126/sciadv.aec8647.abstract: Ongoing and planned hydroelectric dam construction in the Andes will alter water and sediment delivery to downstream rivers, with likely substantial impacts on river and floodplain morphology, hydrology, and habitats. These disturbances will be greatest along laterally dynamic rivers with strong current channel-floodplain coupling, such as Andean foreland rivers. Using a hydro-morphodynamic river model, we show that these floodplains are rapidly transformed through widespread vertical and lateral erosion with persisting long-term effects: Erosion creates secondary floodplains entrenched several meters below pre-dam levels within a century. This degradation of the channel-floodplain complex changes floodplain inundation patterns and frequency and disconnects riparian water bodies from the active river. Such decoupling will be most severe in rivers characterized by high sediment loads and lateral migration rates before dam construction. Our simulations reveal that predictive approaches that neglect geomorphic changes, including lateral river mobility, may be of limited utility in assessing dam impacts on the construction and functioning of wetland habitats.

10.1126/sciadv.aeh0436.title: Unifying energy and information harvesting for high-rate self-powered sensing
10.1126/sciadv.aeh0436.abstract: High-fidelity sensing remains highly challenging in self-powered systems, as the limited power of energy harvesters constrains data acquisition and transmission. In this work, we present a wireless, intelligent, self-powered environmental node (WISE-Node) that simultaneously harvests energy and collects sensing information from ambient vibrations. Its multi-contact triboelectric vibration energy harvester (MC-TVEH) achieves an ultra-wide bandwidth of 10-300 Hz, delivering peak and RMS power densities of 13.42 kW/m 3 and 1.73 kW/m 3 , respectively. The WISE-Node also functions as a broadband sensor, accurately tracking excitation frequencies via FFT analysis ( R 2 = 0.9997 across 3-10,000 Hz). Using a Random Forest classifier on the acquired data, the WISE-Node identifies flange conditions with 99.38% accuracy. Field tests on marine engines and generators validate its robust performance, achieving a cold start in just 28.8 s and maintaining fully self-powered 1000 Hz sampling and stable wireless transmission. These results highlight the proposed WISE-Node’s strong potential for self-sustained high-fidelity sensing, thereby advancing next-generation battery-free industrial IoT and digital twin technologies.

10.1126/sciadv.aef1579.title: The CENP-A chaperone complex spatially organizes centromeres
10.1126/sciadv.aef1579.abstract: Centromeres, defined by CENP-A-containing nucleosomes, direct kinetochore assembly for spindle attachment. In mitosis, CENP-A and the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) of the inner kinetochore are arranged into bipartite subdomains within clearings of chromatin. However, less is known about their architecture during interphase. We report here an unrecognized structural role for the CENP-A chaperone machinery in establishing interphase centromere architecture. In interphase, CENP-A and the CCAN assemble conserved shell-like structures that enclose a chromatin-poor central cavity. This cavity is occupied by the interphase-specific CENP-A chaperone complex, which promotes CENP-A assembly once per cell cycle. The presence of the chaperone complex, but not its CENP-A-incorporating activity, is required to generate both the shell architecture and chromatin clearing. The CCAN scaffold CENP-C exhibits radial organization throughout the structure and is essential for its formation, primarily by recruiting the HJURP chaperone. Our findings broaden the role of the CENP-A chaperone machinery to include the structural organization of interphase vertebrate centromeres, independent of CENP-A deposition.

10.1126/sciadv.adz0039.title: An in situ forming immunomodulatory hydrogel reinvigorates exhausted CD8+ T cells via preserving their mitochondrial fitness
10.1126/sciadv.adz0039.abstract: CD8 + T cell exhaustion driven by mitochondrial dysfunction remains a major barrier to effective cancer immunotherapy. Here, we report an in situ forming d -α-tocopheryl polyethylene glycol succinate (TPGS)-based hydrogel [multifunctional thermosensitive composite gel (MTC Gel)] that reinvigorates exhausted CD8 + T cells by preserving mitochondrial fitness through a two-pronged strategy. After intratumoral injection, MTC Gel rapidly undergoes gelation at physiological temperature and dissociates to generate a high local concentration of TPGS, which targets cancer cell mitochondria to trigger prodeath mitophagy. This process induces robust immunogenic cell death (ICD) and blocks tunneling nanotube-mediated mitochondrial hijacking. Meanwhile, NLG919-loaded hybrid nanoparticles released from MTC Gel synergistically restore mitochondrial biogenesis in CD8 + T cells suppressed by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1. Across multiple murine tumor models, MTC Gel reprograms T cell immunity by reducing CD8 + T cells exhaustion while enhancing effector and cytotoxic functions, thereby eliciting potent tumoricidal activity. These findings highlight this rationally designed hydrogel system as a clinically translatable platform for next-generation ICD-based cancer immunotherapies.
authors: Yiming Qi, Jing Li, Ziyan Chen, Chenming Zou, Haichao Zhu, Alice Shen Yi Shan, Yuli Fu, Jingwen Hou, Chaozhu Zheng, Qiongzhe Ren, Yu Qiao, Zhu Jin, Feihu Wang, Shengrong Guo

10.1126/sciadv.aea1431.title: NRF2 coordinates cystine import and glutathione use to sustain ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance in cancer
10.1126/sciadv.aea1431.abstract: Cancer cells must balance detoxification of reactive metabolic by-products while preserving redox homeostasis, but how this trade-off is managed remains unclear. The Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (KEAP1)-nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) pathway, a key regulator of antioxidant defenses, is frequently hyperactivated in cancer. Formaldehyde, a genotoxic one-carbon by-product, is typically detoxified via glutathione (GSH), which is also essential for suppressing ferroptotic cell death. Here, we show that NRF2 promotes formaldehyde tolerance through up-regulation of the cystine transporter SLC7A11, enabling a protective mechanism that is largely independent of GSH, which remains necessary for ferroptosis resistance. In NRF2-active cells, formaldehyde reacts with cysteine to form a thiazolidine conjugate, and the combination of formaldehyde stress and SLC7A11 inhibition activates the integrated stress response, suppresses global protein synthesis, and markedly compromises cell viability. Together, these findings reveal that NRF2 coordinates ferroptosis resistance and formaldehyde tolerance, exposing a cancer vulnerability through combined inhibition of cystine uptake and GSH synthesis.
authors: Agustín E. Morellato, Natividad Alquezar-Artieda, Alejandro Guerrero-Maldonado, Rajinder Singh, Lilla Beja, Carla Umansky, Laura Perich-Pallaruelo, Mireia Pellicer, Paula Fernandez-Deu, Nicolas Aira, Nour Bourached-Silva, Uciel Chorostecki, Donald J. L. Jones, Gaël Roué, Richard J. Hopkinson, Lucas B. Pontel

10.1126/sciadv.aeb8595.title: Primary tumor-derived lactate primes prostate cancer cells for a dormant fate
10.1126/sciadv.aeb8595.abstract: The metastatic outcome depends on the state of disseminated cancer cells (DCCs) leading to overt metastasis or undergoing dormancy. Before distant organ colonization, primary tumor microenvironment may shape the decision between proliferation and dormancy. Here, we identify lactic acid (LA), a highly abundant environmental metabolite at the primary site in prostate cancer (PCa), as a key inducer of dormant state. LA-uploading PCa cells undergo a proliferation delay, associated with stemness, therapy tolerance, and invasiveness through the nuclear receptor subfamily 2 group F member 1 (COUP-TF1/NR2F1) activation. These traits rely on LA-driven accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), which serve as reservoirs of lipid-derived acetyl moieties essential for histone acetylation. Notably, the epigenetic reader BRD4 is essential for COUP-TF1 expression and for establishing and maintaining dormancy. In metastatic sites, where LA levels are low, dormant features are lost, allowing DCCs to support metastatic growth. Last, targeting LA-mediated LD formation or BRD4 activation prevents dormancy entry, reducing PCa cell adaptability and increasing vulnerability to antiproliferative therapies.
authors: Luigi Ippolito, Erica Pranzini, Giulia Gangarossa, Marta Iozzo, Giuseppina Comito, Giacomo Venditti, Sara Roccabianca, Elisa Pardella, Matteo Lulli, Alice Santi, Gabriella Nesi, Elisa Giannoni, Paola Chiarugi

10.1126/sciadv.aeb9836.title: CASTOR1 functional inactivation drives KRAS-mutant NSCLC and therapy resistance by a noncanonical mechanism of tumor suppression
10.1126/sciadv.aeb9836.abstract: CASTOR1, a cytosolic arginine sensor and regulator of mTORC1 signaling, is identified here as a tumor suppressor in KRAS -driven non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In a KRAS G12D mouse model, CASTOR1 deletion enhances tumor initiation and progression, accompanied by increased proliferation. Although CASTOR1 is rarely mutated or deleted in human cancers, its expression progressively declines during tumor progression and is associated with increased AKT activation and CASTOR1 phosphorylation, consistent with functional inactivation. Loss of CASTOR1 results in constitutive mTORC1 hyperactivation, impaired arginine-dependent regulation of mTORC1 signaling, elevated p-4EBP1 and p-S6 levels, increased AKT and ERK activation, genomic instability, and resistance to KRAS G12D inhibitors. Tumors and tumor-derived organoids deficient in CASTOR1 are resistant to KRAS inhibition, but this resistance can be overcome by cotargeting mTORC1 or dual PI3K/mTOR inhibition. These findings identify CASTOR1 as a critical link between nutrient sensing and oncogenic signaling and reveal its functional inactivation as an important mechanism contributing to KRAS -driven NSCLC progression and therapeutic resistance. The results further support rational combination therapies to overcome KRAS inhibitor resistance in CASTOR1-low NSCLC.
authors: Xian Wang, Ling Ding, Wen Meng, Elaine Byrnes, Suet Kee Loo, Shenyu Sun, Luping Chen, Tingting Li, Man-Tzu Wang, Arjun Pennathur, Yufei Huang, Shou-Jiang Gao

10.1126/sciadv.aee0560.title: Lineage-specific and gestational age-dependent DNA methylation programming orchestrates human placental development
10.1126/sciadv.aee0560.abstract: The human placenta is essential for pregnancy, yet the dynamic regulation of its DNA methylome during development remains poorly understood. To address this, we generated a single base-resolution DNA methylation atlas of human placental trophoblasts across gestation. We identified a lineage-specific methylation program established immediately after implantation, followed by gestational age-dependent methylation accumulation. This program acted as a developmental barrier that coordinated placental maturation and immune homeostasis. By integrating histone modifications and functional perturbations, we revealed a temporal dynamic between H3K27me3 and DNA methylation that silenced proinflammatory loci and a switch from H3K9me3 to DNA methylation at repeat elements to maintain genome stability. Aberrant methylation in preterm placentas underscored the physiological importance of methylation regulation. Using human trophoblast stem cells, we demonstrated that DNMT1 was critically required for maintaining trophoblast methylome integrity and self-renewal, while the DNMT3 family were equally essential for trophoblast survival. Overall, we established a placenta-specific epigenetic framework for human trophoblast development.

10.1126/sciadv.aee3876.title: PhagoID: Quantitative in situ proximity labeling defines the proteomes of bead- and microbe-containing phagosome lumina across species, maturation, and immune activation
10.1126/sciadv.aee3876.abstract: The phagosome is an immune organelle that integrates signals from diverse cargos to drive pathogen killing, tissue homeostasis, and antigen presentation. How this compartment coordinates such diverse functions remains incompletely understood. A comprehensive view of phagosomal composition across cell states and perturbations could accelerate insight into its regulation. Here, we establish PhagoID, a modular proximity labeling approach that enables in situ proteomic profiling of the phagosome lumen in living cells. Applying PhagoID to murine and human macrophages, we define conserved and species-specific phagosomal proteomes that include both canonical lysosomal components and unexpected contributors from nuclear, mitochondrial, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) compartments. Integrating these proteomes with 25 genome-scale CRISPR screens of phagosomal phenotypes, we identify a network of lumenal proteins that regulate cargo uptake, acidification, antigen presentation, and microbial control highlighting previously unrecognized phagosomal effectors. We next adapt PhagoID to profile the microbe-containing phagosome and compare the sterile bead-containing phagosome to the Escherichia coli -containing phagosome, demonstrating a modest E. coli signature of phagosome remodeling. Comparative analyses further reveal that loss of LAMP1 enhances recruitment of ER-derived proteins to the phagosome, whereas loss of TFEB minimally perturbs the lumenal proteome despite its role in lysosomal biogenesis. Last, cytokine stimulation remodels the phagosome lumen to enrich for proteins involved in antigen presentation and antimicrobial activity in response to type I and II interferons. These data demonstrate that PhagoID delivers a high-confidence, quantitative, and integrative map of the phagosome lumen, revealing previously unidentified axes of organellar communication and regulatory control in innate immunity.
authors: Benjamin L. Allsup, Supriya Gharpure, Cal Gunnarsson, Mateo L. Stagg, Bryan D. Bryson

10.1126/sciadv.aee4738.title: SCML2 inhibits PrimPol-mediated DNA replication repriming and regulates replication gap-associated cancer cell vulnerability
10.1126/sciadv.aee4738.abstract: PrimPol-mediated fork repriming generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps during DNA damage tolerance (DDT), which, if not properly repaired, can threaten genomic stability. PrimPol is a highly error-prone polymerase. Thus, PrimPol activity should be tightly regulated to fit into DDT and remain low during unstressed DNA replication. Human sex comb on midleg like-2 (SCML2), a Polycomb protein containing MBT repeats, has been identified as a component of the noncanonical PRC1 complex and a regulator of p53 and CHK1 stability. Here, we show that SCML2A is a suppressor of PrimPol. SCML2A directly binds two domains of PrimPol: Its RBR domain binds the C terminus of PrimPol, and its SAM domain binds the amino-terminal AEP domain, thereby inhibiting ssDNA-binding capacity of the AEP domain. SCML2 depletion leads to increased nascent DNA synthesis and accumulation of PrimPol-mediated ssDNA gaps under replication stress. SCML2 depletion also enhances PrimPol engagement during unstressed DNA replication, leading to subsequent accumulation of ssDNA gaps, which are filled by REV1/POLζ-mediated translesion synthesis (TLS) and RAD51-mediated template switching (TS). SCML2 depletion confers cellular hypersensitivity to RAD51 or REV1/POLζ inhibition, which is associated with increased accumulation of ssDNA gaps. Furthermore, CDK2 phosphorylates SCML2A at Ser 267 , which suppresses RBR-mediated PrimPol interaction. Cyclin E1 overexpression leads to CDK2-mediated SCML2A Ser 267 hyperphosphorylation, which releases the inhibitory effect of SCML2A on PrimPol and subsequently induces ssDNA gap accumulation. Collectively, we identify SCML2A as a negative regulator of PrimPol.
authors: Xin Shi, Qianqian Peng, Jing Guo, Wei Wu, Ping Wang, Xin Zhou, Qiang Chen

10.1126/sciadv.aee5135.title: Scalable architecture for measurement-induced squeezed light interferometers
10.1126/sciadv.aee5135.abstract: Scalable interferometers lie at the heart of photonic quantum technologies, but their expansion has been fundamentally limited by optical losses that grow with circuit depth. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a measurement-induced architecture for multimode squeezed-light interferometers that overcomes this barrier. By shifting complexity from deep optical networks to programmable homodyne measurements, we realize effective transformations within a shallow, low-loss platform. We validate the principle with a six-mode device and extend it to a 400-mode interferometer, marking a leap in scale beyond conventional designs. Crucially, this strategy not only enables scalable squeezed light interferometry but also provides a powerful route to the generation of large-scale entangled states-a key requirement for quantum computing, simulation, and communication. Our results establish measurement-induced circuits as a practical pathway toward noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) applications and future demonstrations of quantum advantage.
authors: Abhinav Verma, Jacob Hastrup, Jonas S. Neergaard-Nielsen, Ulrik L. Andersen

10.1126/sciadv.aee5241.title: RAF isoform selectivity of MEK inhibitors and rational design of a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor
10.1126/sciadv.aee5241.abstract: Aberrant activation of the RAS/RAF/mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway is a frequent cause of cancer. Allosteric MEK inhibitors block this pathway by binding RAF-MEK complexes to prevent activation of MEK by RAF. However, how MEK inhibitor potency varies across the three RAF isoforms remains poorly understood. We profiled seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and observed a notable hierarchy of sensitivity: All most potently inhibited CRAF-driven MEK activation while relatively sparing ARAF-driven activation. We identified point mutations in ARAF and CRAF proximate to the MEK inhibitor binding site that markedly altered inhibitor sensitivity. Using a rational design approach, we developed a more potent inhibitor of ARAF-driven MEK signaling, TWG-07-148. Our cryo-electron microscopy structure shows how this acrylamide-containing analog of MEK inhibitor trametinib covalently targets Cys 514 , a residue unique to ARAF. Our studies highlight the importance of the activating RAF isoform as a determinant of MEK inhibitor sensitivity and provide proof of concept for the development of MEK inhibitors that more effectively block ARAF-driven MEK signaling via covalent targeting of Cys 514 .
authors: Sayan Chakraborty, Jie Jiang, Javier Vinals Camallonga, Dimitris Gazgalis, Thomas W. Gero, Maurício T. Tavares, Georgia Dittemore, Emre Tkacik, Tyler S. Beyett, Dong Man Jang, Byung Hak Ha, Felix H. Gottlieb, Talya Levitz, Rebecca J. Metivier, Anna M. Schmoker, David A. Scott, Hyesung Jeon, Pasi A. Jänne, Michael J. Eck

10.1126/sciadv.aee9670.title: Histone methyltransferase NSD2 shapes CD8+ T cell fates through the H3K36me2-Zbtb20 axis
10.1126/sciadv.aee9670.abstract: CD8 + T cells, as the most important cytolytic cells in adaptive immunity, can differentiate into distinct subpopulations with specific functions and fates. During this process, CD8 + T cells exhibit substantial plasticity in their differentiation trajectory. Notably, epigenetic regulation has emerged as a pivotal mechanism to govern T cell fate decisions. In this study, we demonstrate that the histone methyltransferase NSD2 critically regulates CD8 + T cell differentiation during acute viral infection. While NSD2 deficiency enhances the early expansion of activated CD8 + T cells, it severely compromises their survival fitness during the contraction phase, leading to a disproportionate collapse of the antigen-specific pool and limiting the establishment of robust long-lived memory. Mechanistically, this defect is driven by the disruption of the H3K36me2- Zbtb20 regulatory axis. Furthermore, we show that in the absence of NSD2, CD8 + T cells in tumor exhibit an increased proportion but dysfunctional resident memory T cell phenotype. Collectively, our findings highlight a critical role for NSD2 in providing more mechanistic insights into how epigenetic mechanisms fine-tune T cell differentiation.
authors: Shijie Yuan, Yifan Xu, Huicheng Liu, Ying Xue, Mengdi Zhu, Xiaorong Xie, Xuwei Wu, Yuting Xia, Lin Li, Yuan Luo, Zehan Huang, Xiangping Yang, Huiyun Du, Ran He

10.1126/sciadv.aef2844.title: High-throughput droplet-based enzymatic DNA methylome profiling enables single-cell resolution of epigenetic heterogeneity
10.1126/sciadv.aef2844.abstract: DNA methylation is a fundamental epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression, cellular identity, and disease-associated regulatory programs. However, high-throughput single-cell DNA methylation technologies have been limited by DNA degradation, low CpG recovery, and the poor scalability of bisulfite-based methods. Here, we present scEM-seq, a droplet-based single-cell enzymatic methylome sequencing method that integrates barcode ligation within a single emulsification step, followed by postemulsion cytosine-to-uracil conversion. This design substantially reduces DNA loss and enables robust profiling of tens of thousands of single cells per experiment. scEM-seq generates high-quality single-cell methylomes with moderately improved CpG coverage and balanced read utilization compared with other droplet-based microfluidic methods. Applied to peripheral blood mononuclear cells, scEM-seq accurately resolves major immune lineages, and in prostate cancer tissues, it reveals diverse malignant cell states and patient-specific epigenetic and copy number architectures. scEM-seq enables scalable single-cell dissection of epigenetic heterogeneity across diverse biological and disease contexts, broadening the scope of DNA methylation-based studies into cellular regulation and disease.
authors: Gaojie Li, Yang Yang, Zhuoran Li, Qi Wang, Ying Wang, Bin Guo, Kunmeng Yang, Ming Tan, Jinwei Li, Jiacheng Sun, Guangxin Zhang, Shengwei Xiong, Mei Zhang, Zhihua Zhang, Yingying Xie, Yue Shi, Xin Ma, Weimin Ci

10.1126/sciadv.aef6029.title: Loss of KAT5-dependent H2A.Z acetylation provokes chromosomal instability in recurrent pregnancy loss
10.1126/sciadv.aef6029.abstract: Placenta defects are one of the major causes of miscarriages, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We demonstrate that trophoblast-specific depletion of the acetyltransferase Kat5 , or introduction of acetylation-defective mutants Kat5-Q377E G380E and Kat5-Y47A , induces severe chromosomal instability (CIN) during trophoblast cells division, leading to embryonic lethality. Moreover, mutation of a key lysine acetyltransferase 5 (KAT5) substrate, H2A.Z, via the introduction of H2az1-K5R K8R K12R K14R (which prevents H2A.Z acetylation), phenocopies the effects of KAT5 loss. Integrated RNA sequencing and CUT&Tag in mouse trophoblast stem cells reveal that KAT5, through H2A.Z acetylation, regulates transcription of key mitotic genes ( Aurka , Aurkb , and Cenpa ). We extend our finding to human trophoblast stem cells, demonstrating a conserved role for KAT5 in preventing CIN. Clinical analysis of placental villi from recurrent pregnancy loss patients with copy number variations revealed reduced expression of KAT5 and acetylated H2A.Z. This study demonstrates that the conserved KAT5-H2A.Z acetylation pathway safeguards chromosomal stability in trophoblast cells, supporting placenta development and successful pregnancy.
authors: Shilei Bi, Yongjie Chen, Lizi Zhang, Jiahui Zhang, Yijing Wang, Baoying Huang, Shanze Li, Lijun Huang, Yifan Wang, Huarong Wang, Ranran Meng, Zhaowei Tu, Lili Du, Haibin Wang, Zhijian Wang, Dunjin Chen, Shuang Zhang, Fengchao Wang

10.1126/sciadv.aef8067.title: Direct observations of submesoscale turbulence driving mesoscale eddy leakage
10.1126/sciadv.aef8067.abstract: Understanding oceanic transport and material fate has long relied on observations that primarily resolve mesoscale, largely geostrophic flows, leaving the role of submesoscale turbulence comparatively unobserved and poorly understood. Here, using new high-resolution drifter-cluster experiments with closest initial spacings below 1 km, we provide direct Lagrangian observations of how submesoscale turbulence modifies mesoscale eddy coherence and transport pathways. The clustered drifters resolve intense, transient ageostrophic motions that are fundamentally absent from geostrophic descriptions of eddy behavior. Analyzed in an eddy-centered reference frame, the observations reveal pronounced submesoscale-driven radial dispersion that facilitates substantial water-mass exchange between the eddy core and its periphery in both the mixed layer and the subsurface. Quantitative estimates indicate submesoscale horizontal diffusivity of O (10 to 100) m 2 /s and a nonlocal dispersion regime across submesoscales. These results challenge the traditional view of mesoscale eddies as coherent structures containing a persistent water mass, with broad implications for interpreting and predicting the transport and fate of tracers in the ocean.
authors: Haijin Cao, Zhiyou Jing, Baylor Fox-Kemper, Bo Qiu, Joseph H. Lacasce, Tong Yan

10.1126/sciadv.aeg4557.title: Morphological intelligence for dynamic aerial interactions
10.1126/sciadv.aeg4557.abstract: Biological flyers achieve ecological dominance not through flight alone, but by seamlessly integrating aerial locomotion with forceful physical interactions, including snatching prey, perching on irregular surfaces, and operating across diverse media. Translating this agility into aerial robotics demands reconciling a fundamental conflict: impulsive, high-force actions destabilize the flight platform. Here, we present a bio-inspired unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) equipped with a mechanically intelligent impulsive limb that resolves this tradeoff through physical decoupling. An asymmetric bistable impulse module delivers a 2.3-fold extension within 70 ms, while a soft-linkage architecture reduces the transmission of impulsive interaction forces to the airframe. For the tested seven-segment configuration, intrinsic geometric tolerance corresponds to a passive vertical accommodation range of approximately 70% of the fully deployed arm length, reducing the need for precise altitude regulation within the tested range. We demonstrate the system’s multimodal capacity through dynamic in-flight snatching, energy-efficient perching, high-impact solid fracture, and cross-medium capture in viscous fluids, establishing a new paradigm for UAVs executing physically demanding tasks in complex environments.
authors: Yongkang Jiang, Junjin Li, Shuyu Meng, Yanmin Zhou, Bin He, Jamie Paik

10.1126/sciadv.aeg5840.title: Structural basis for start codon selection by eIF5-mimic proteins
10.1126/sciadv.aeg5840.abstract: Start codon selection extensively regulates the cellular proteome and is implicated in cancer and other diseases. The eIF5-mimic proteins (5MPs: 5MP1/BZW2 and 5MP2/BZW2) restrict non-AUG start codon usage and thereby reprogram proteoform expression from mRNAs with alternative start sites, such as the oncogenic c-Myc. Here, using in extracto cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and biochemical assays, we report how 5MP represses translation dependent on the sequence context at start codons. Cryo-EM structures of 48 S preinitiation complexes (PICs) reveal 5MP1 bound at the A site of the small ribosomal subunit. 5MPs act as initiation factors that stabilize an open PIC conformation, promoting mRNA scanning and inhibiting initiation at suboptimal start codons. We propose to designate 5MP as eIF1S (eukaryotic initiation factor 1 scanning). These findings reveal the structural basis for proteome modulation by 5MPs and may help correct dysregulated translation in disease.

10.1126/sciadv.aeg8654.title: Using initial states to identify successful El Niño-Southern Oscillation forecasts 1 year in advance
10.1126/sciadv.aeg8654.abstract: El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the primary source of climate predictability on seasonal and longer timescales over much of the globe, but predicting its phase beyond 9 months has remained challenging. Here, we leverage an underappreciated factor in ENSO forecasting: the substantial variation in forecast skill based on the ENSO phase at the time a forecast is issued. Our analysis of transitions between ENSO phases in a dynamical hindcast dataset demonstrates that this variation markedly exceeds intermodel differences in predictive capability. Forecasts initialized during La Niña conditions perform best, with three models correctly predicting transitions to El Niño 1 year in advance over 70% of the time. We present our findings in a simple framework that allows decision-makers to assess the likelihood of a forecast being correct on the basis of the current ENSO state. Applied effectively, these findings could improve long-lead ENSO forecasting strategies, enhancing global risk management.
authors: Nandini Ramesh, Mandy B. Freund, Damien B. Irving, Dougal T. Squire, Carly R. Tozer, Didier P. Monselesan, Tess Parker, Annette Stellema, James S. Risbey

10.1126/sciadv.aeg9427.title: Hemolymph pressure-mediated friction in the tarsus of the desert locust (Schistocerca gregaria)
10.1126/sciadv.aeg9427.abstract: The desert locust ( Schistocerca gregaria ) performs high-acceleration jumps within milliseconds, relying not only on powerful muscles and spring-loaded hindlegs, but also on precise tarsi-substrate interactions. Although the mechanics of jumping have been extensively studied, the mechanisms enabling rapid attachment and detachment remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize the frictional properties of hindleg tarsi under controlled low-speed contact conditions targeting selected loading features associated with jumping. We hypothesize that locusts coordinate tarsal cuticular structures with internal hemolymph pressure to modulate contact mechanics. Using high-speed videography, a suite of advanced microscopic techniques, biomechanical experiments, and biomimetic prototypes, we provide evidence that hemolymph pressure modulates tarsal stiffness and acts together with structural asymmetry to produce direction-dependent frictional responses. This interplay may contribute to adaptive friction tuning associated with jumping. Our findings advance the understanding of locust locomotor biomechanics and suggest design principles for robotic systems requiring rapid and controllable surface engagement.
authors: Jiahui Zhao, Zhendong Dai, Stanislav N. Gorb, Chuchu Li

10.1126/sciadv.aeh1073.title: Interferon-λ signaling to maternal dendritic cells protects against congenital Zika virus infection
10.1126/sciadv.aeh1073.abstract: Interferon-λ (IFN-λ, type III IFN) mediates antiviral immunity at anatomic barriers, including the maternal-fetal interface. To investigate the effects of IFN-λ during congenital Zika virus (ZIKV) infection, we infected mice lacking the IFN-αβ receptor ( Ifnar1 −/− ) or both the IFN-αβ and IFN-λ receptors ( Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− ) at embryonic day 9 and found that loss of maternal IFN-λ signaling resulted in greater transplacental transmission, highlighting a protective effect of IFN-λ at the maternal-fetal interface. To investigate the spatial relationship between ZIKV infection and antiviral responses, we used HiPlex RNAscope on the entire gravid uterus and found that IFN-λ was expressed more proximal to the site of ZIKV infection in Ifnar1 −/− dams compared to Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− dams. We performed immunophenotyping of the placenta and uterus by flow cytometry and found a decrease in dendritic cells and natural killer (NK) cells in the uterus of Ifnar1 −/− Ifnlr1 −/− dams compared to Ifnar1 −/− dams, but NK cell depletion did not affect fetal infection. Using conditional knockout mice, we identified maternal dendritic cells as the key IFN-λ-responsive cell type mediating protection against ZIKV congenital infection. Together, our data support a model in which IFN-λ signaling to maternal dendritic cells increases dendritic cell accumulation in the uterus, which facilitates a protective antiviral response that restricts ZIKV congenital infection.
authors: Margaret R. Dedloff, Thomas R. Reinhardt, Tessa-Jonne F. Ropp, Joel Rivera-Cardona, Celeste R. Robles, Rebecca L. Casazza, J. Ashley Ezzell, Michelle S. Itano, Helen M. Lazear

10.1126/sciadv.aeh3295.title: Frequency-dependent fitness effects are ubiquitous in rapidly adapting microbial populations
10.1126/sciadv.aeh3295.abstract: In simple microbial populations, the fitness effects of selected mutations are typically assumed to be constant, regardless of mutant frequency. This assumption underpins predictions about evolutionary dynamics, epistasis, and the maintenance of genetic diversity. Here, we systematically test this assumption using beneficial mutations from early generations of the Escherichia coli long-term evolution experiment (LTEE). Using flow cytometry-based competition assays, we find that frequency-dependent fitness effects are the norm rather than the exception, occurring in ∼80% of strain pairs tested. Most competitions exhibit negative frequency dependence, where fitness advantages decline as mutant frequency increases. We demonstrate that the strength of frequency dependence is predictable from invasion fitness measurements, which explain approximately half of the biological variation in frequency-dependent slopes. We also observe violations of fitness transitivity in several strain combinations, indicating that competitive outcomes cannot always be predicted from fitness measured against a single reference strain. High-resolution measurements reveal that frequency dependence changes substantially within the growth cycle, with the net per-cycle effect reflecting the balance of opposing dynamics at different growth phases. Our results demonstrate that, even in a model system designed to minimize ecological complexity, subtle interactions between closely related genotypes create frequency-dependent selection that can fundamentally alter evolutionary trajectories.
authors: Joao A. Ascensao, Keon D. Abedi, Aditya N. Prasad, Oskar Hallatschek

10.1126/sciadv.aeh5101.title: Electrically reconfigurable dipolar polaritons with highly tunable nonlinearity in a homobilayer microcavity
10.1126/sciadv.aeh5101.abstract: Active control over optical nonlinearity in solid-state systems is central to unlocking exotic many-body phenomena and photonic devices. While exciton-polaritons in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer a promising platform, their practical utility is impeded by fixed interactions and a trade-off between nonlinearity and oscillator strength. Here, we report electrically tunable dipolar polaritons in a dual-gated bilayer MoS 2 microcavity, demonstrating in situ reshaping of the dispersion and modulation of the light-matter coupling strength via the quantum-confined Stark effect. Crucially, this electrical control yields a seven-fold enhancement of the polariton-polariton interaction strength. This enhancement arises from the combined tuning of the effective exciton-exciton interaction and the excitonic Hopfield coefficient. In addition, electrostatic doping provides an independent knob to continuously drive a strong-to-weak coupling crossover. Our findings establish dual-gated TMD homobilayer as a versatile platform for on-chip, dynamically reconfigurable nonlinear light-matter physics.
authors: Baixu Xiang, Yubin Wang, Guihan Wen, Yitong Li, Hao Wen, Zengde She, Haiyun Liu, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Timothy C. H. Liew, Zhiyuan Sun, Qihua Xiong

10.1126/sciadv.aeh5116.title: Bioinspired ventral-groove fibers for volume-programmable pneumatic actuation
10.1126/sciadv.aeh5116.abstract: Pneumatic actuation plays a central role in soft robotics, with conventional systems relying on pressure-driven chamber deformation and closed-loop feedback for precise control. Here, we introduce bioinspired ventral-groove filamentary fibers that reframe pneumatic actuation from pressure-dominated chambers to volume-programmable fiber architectures, enabling previously unexplored robotic capabilities. Coupling microgroove unfolding with elastic expansion, these molecularly programmed fibers achieve reversible 400× area expansion at ultralow pressure (∼0.8 kPa) and scale from ∼100 μm to centimeter-scale diameters and tens of meters in length, supporting micro- to macro-scale robotic systems. We demonstrate responsive textile actuation through an everyday flotation garment with 20-m fibers seamlessly integrated into clothing. We also show a gripping approach with three capabilities: disturbance-robust high-precision grasping, conformal handling of fragile nerve-like filaments and delicate incense-ash cones, and open-loop operation that reduces reliance on sensory feedback. By establishing a volume-programmable actuation paradigm, this work paves the way for low-pressure pneumatic technologies in soft robotics and responsive textiles.
authors: Xiaoyu Zhang, Qianyi Li, Xiaolong Li, Ziang Li, Haoran Qiu, Shiyun Qian, Ying Yi Tan, Hong Yee Low, Tural Khudiyev

10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128.title: Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM
10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128.abstract: Anatomically modern humans first settled in Europe at least 45,000 years ago, yet limited genomic data from 45 to 20 thousand years (ka) constrain reconstructions of Upper Palaeolithic population dynamics. Before the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM; ∼26.5 to 19 ka), Gravettian groups (∼34 to 25 ka) were widespread across Europe and genetically diverse, including the Fournol and Věstonice lineages. Here, we present genome-wide data from three Gravettian individuals: two from the Franco-Cantabrian region (Chufín, Spain, and Isturitz, France) and one from Italy (Ostuni1b). Our analyses reveal previously undetected gene flow between eastern and western early Gravettian populations in southwestern Europe, challenging models of regional genetic continuity from the Aurignacian to the Solutrean (∼24 to 19 ka). To investigate population history during the LGM, a period for which human skeletal remains are extremely rare, we analyzed sedimentary ancient DNA from Solutrean Layer 122 at El Mirón Cave (Cantabria, Spain; ∼22,000 calibrated years before the present), recovering ∼14,000 human single-nucleotide polymorphisms. These data support persistence of Fournol-related ancestry in southwestern Europe throughout the LGM.
authors: Pere Gelabert, Susanna Sawyer, Vanessa Villalba-Mouco, Olivia Cheronet, Victoria Oberreiter, Diego Gárate, Christian Normand, Lawrence G. Straus, Manuel R. 10.1126/sciadv.aeh6590.title: In situ CAR-M engineered by liposomal mRNA nanomedicine remodels fibrotic microenvironment for ameliorating liver fibrosis
10.1126/sciadv.aeh6590.abstract: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)-incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)-CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.
authors: Hong Xiao, Xiaoxia Li, Kaimin Cai, Yifei Leng, Xiaoyan Miao, Tinghui Yin, Xintao Shuai, Jie Ren

10.1126/sciadv.aeh6993.title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach
10.1126/sciadv.aeh6993.abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M 3 .I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M 3 .I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M 3 .I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.
authors: Simone Pelicci, Laura Furia, Lorenzo Ciacci, Teresa Gravina, Pier Giuseppe Pelicci, Gaetano Ivan Dellino, Mario Faretta

10.1126/sciadv.aeh7499.title: SMCHD1 loss rewires MYOD1 enhancer nexuses and chromatin accessibility landscapes in muscle cells
10.1126/sciadv.aeh7499.abstract: SMCHD1 is a chromatin architectural protein linked to heterochromatin repression. Loss of function mutations of SMCHD1 cause facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy type 2 (FSHD2) through activation of the DUX4 transcription factor gene. However, it is unknown how SMCHD1 may regulate transcription independently of DUX4. Here, we show that SMCHD1 safeguards enhancer organization within the three-dimensional (3D) genome in human myoblasts. Loss of SMCHD1 leads to widespread gains in chromatin accessibility, aberrant transcription, and selective remodeling of myogenic transcription factor MYOD1 occupancy. Integrative analyses of histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, Hi-C looping, and enhancer-gene modeling reveal that SMCHD1 loss rewires the landscape of clustered enhancers and promotes the emergence of new networks of enhancer elements, termed MYOD1 enhancer nexuses. These structures are marked by increased enhancer connectivity, increased local 3D chromatin interactions, and coordinated activation of genes likely relevant for FSHD pathology. Our findings identify SMCHD1 as a key architectural constraint that suppresses hyperactive enhancer networks, thereby preserving transcriptional homeostasis in myoblasts.
authors: Zhijun Huang, Wei Cui, Adam Klaiss, Gerd P. Pfeifer

10.1126/sciadv.aei0758.title: The Nematostella synaptonemal complex mediates divergent and sex-specific meiotic programs
10.1126/sciadv.aei0758.abstract: Throughout eukaryotes, the synaptonemal complex (SC) is a supramolecular structure essential for meiotic chromosome dynamics and sexual reproduction. While metazoan SC proteins display substantial sequence divergence, the lack of functional analyses beyond bilaterian models has obscured a mechanistic understanding of SC evolution. Here, we report that the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis exhibits synapsis of homologous chromosomes in a classic zipper-like manner and expresses at least eight orthologs of 10 known vertebrate SC proteins. Unexpectedly, mutagenesis of the core SC components sycp1 , syce2 , and sycp3 resulted in divergent and sexually dimorphic phenotypes, indicating the functional diversification of these conserved factors. Combined, these findings challenge the assumption that the conservation of protein sequence or ultrastructure implies mechanistic homology.
authors: Stefanie Williams, Jennifer Gardner, Stephanie H. Nowotarski, Matthew C. Gibson

10.1126/sciadv.aei1547.title: A methylation-dependent reader couples arginine methylation to S6K2 signaling in vivo
10.1126/sciadv.aei1547.abstract: Arginine methylation regulates diverse cellular processes, yet how methyl-arginine reader proteins couple this modification to kinase signaling in vivo remains poorly defined. Here, we identify staphylococcal nuclease and Tudor domain containing 1 (SND1) as a pancreas-enriched effector that links symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) recognition to S6 kinase 2 (S6K2) activation. Disruption of SDMA-mediated binding by a point mutation in the SND1 Tudor domain markedly diminishes ribosomal protein S6 (S6) phosphorylation in the pancreas. Mechanistically, SND1 engages SDMA-modified arginines within the carboxyl-terminal glycine-arginine-rich (GAR) motif of S6K2 and promotes S6K2-dependent S6 phosphorylation. Mice harboring lysine substitutions at these GAR arginines ( S6k2 RK) phenocopy Snd1 Tudor-mutant ( Snd1 knock-in) animals, exhibiting impaired pancreatic S6 phosphorylation. Transcriptomic analyses reveal extensive overlap in dysregulated pathways between Snd1 and S6k2 mutant pancreata, supporting a shared signaling cascade. Together, these findings establish a methylation-dependent reader-kinase axis that links protein arginine methyltransferase 5-catalyzed arginine methylation to tissue-specific control of ribosome signaling and cellular stress adaptation.
authors: Yalong Wang, Bin Liu, Rongjie Fu, Wei He, Daniel J. McGrail, Han Xu, Mark T. Bedford

10.1126/sciadv.aei2880.title: Spider-inspired bidirectional robotic joints driven by electrohydraulic multiaxial strain
10.1126/sciadv.aei2880.abstract: Compared with conventional motors and servos, soft-actuated angular-motion devices are superior in environmental adaptability and human-robot interaction, yet they can only achieve active bidirectional angular motion by integrating antagonistic actuators or restriction modules. The integration of such components introduces deformation antagonism, compromises structural simplicity, and increases control complexity. Herein, we propose a spider-inspired centimeter-scale soft bidirectional robotic joint driven by a pair of synchronously controlled electrohydraulic actuators (EHAs). Specifically, the EHAs generate multiaxial strain, enabling the joint to bidirectionally rotate depending on its physical state, without introducing additional functional components or asynchronous controllers. Furthermore, the joint demonstrates (i) high-speed (forward: 2851° per second, reverse: 1934° per second) and wide-stroke (up to 156.8°) rotational performance, (ii) multimodal motion (e.g., self-unfolding, self-folding, and reciprocating swinging), (iii) continuous response (up to 40 hertz), and (iv) payload-bearing capability. Last, three joint-integrated devices validate its feasibility as a multifunctional, high-dynamic, and single-channel-controlled actuation component in diverse robotic applications. This work establishes a viable design framework for minimalist yet versatile bioinspired robots.
authors: Zean Yuan, Shuhong Huang, Luna Zhou, Xinyu Zhu, Jun Luo, Guo Zhan Lum, Rui Chen

10.1126/sciadv.aej1008.title: A noncanonical meiotic cohesin complex associates with specific MCM complexes to promote cohesion establishment and homolog bias
10.1126/sciadv.aej1008.abstract: A meiosis-specific cohesin complex is essential for the segregation of homologous chromosomes and sister chromatids during meiosis, yet its composition and mechanism in Drosophila remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that SOLO directly interacts with SUNN, SSEP, and SMC1 and that these interactions are conserved between Drosophila melanogaster and Zeugodacus cucurbitae , a Tephritidae species within Diptera. SOLO associates with SMC1 via specific conserved residues within its highly conserved carboxyl-terminal domain. Furthermore, SOLO directly interacts with the MCM4 and MCM6 subunits of the MCM complex and with MMS22L to establish cohesion; consequently, postreplicative expression of SOLO results in a complete function loss. SOLO also interacts with the MEI-217 and MEI-218 subunits of the meiosis-specific minichromosome maintenance complex to promote homolog bias during meiosis. We propose that in Diptera, an evolutionarily diverged meiotic cohesin complex, composed of SOLO, SUNN, SSEP, SMC1, and SMC3, interacts with various complexes to fulfill its diverse meiotic functions.
authors: Lujie Ma, Qianqian Jin, Dongcheng Hu, Xianwu Lin, Zizhen Fan, Rihui Yan

10.1126/sciadv.adx5564.title: Biophysically constrained learning from healthy neural priors improves motor decoding in pathological cortical networks
10.1126/sciadv.adx5564.abstract: High-performance brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) rely on stable neural representations, yet brain functional impairments inherently disrupt canonical encoding, creating a fundamental decoding paradox. Conventional data-driven approaches struggle to bridge this gap because of pathological data scarcity and heterogeneity. Here, we propose to leverage healthy neural priors and introduce Pathology-Aware Consensus Training (PACT), a paradigm embedding biophysical constraints into healthy neural recordings to guide neural decoding. In a gesture classification task using high-density electrocorticography from patients with gliomas infiltrating the motor cortex, PACT improved the accuracy by more than 10%, effectively restoring the distorted semantic geometry of motor commands and realigning them with healthy canonical representations (correlation increase: r = 0.66 to r = 0.94). Mechanistically, PACT induced an emergent “inverse weighting” strategy: The model autonomously suppresses high-power pathological noise while reanchoring spatial attention to functional compensatory regions. This study provides a proof of concept for improving decoding in compromised networks by harnessing healthy neural dynamics, laying the theoretical foundation for future BCI deployments in clinical populations.
authors: Yihan Wu, Tao Chang, Siliang Chen, Yuxin Quan, Qiang Sun, Marc M. Van Hulle, Yanhui Liu, Ning Jiang, Dario Farina, Yuan Yang, Qing Mao, Jiayuan He

10.1126/sciadv.aeb1963.title: An innovative colon inflammation-targeting platform for ulcerative colitis treatment
10.1126/sciadv.aeb1963.abstract: The therapeutic options for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) have recently expanded substantially. Tofacitinib, an oral small-molecule inhibitor of Janus kinase (JAK), recently FDA approved for ulcerative colitis, represented a paradigm shift in a field previously dominated by biologics. Tofacitinib, however, carries a black box warning for major adverse cardiovascular events, an elevated risk of malignancies, risk of blood clots, and pulmonary embolism. In addition, tofacitinib is avoided in pregnancy and used with caution in women of child bearing age due to potential risks to the developing fetus. Notably, these potential complications are all due to the systemic distribution of tofacitinib. To address these issues, we developed Lipo-tm-HA, a liposomal platform incorporating mannitol (m) and hyaluronic acid (HA) for targeting tofacitinib (t) to the inflamed colon. We characterized Lipo-tm-HA and have shown that it (i) remains stable in gastric conditions due to HA coating, (ii) adheres to transferrin in inflamed mucosa due to its negative charge, and (iii) enhances macrophage uptake through mannose receptor-mediated endocytosis. Due to targeting, we show that a single oral administration of Lipo-tm-HA at a dose of 10 milligrams per kilogram is superior in efficacy compared with daily treatment with free tofacitinib in a dextran sodium sulfate-induced colitis model. Collectively, our innovative formulation will enable colonic inflammation targeting, reduce systemic exposure, and allow administration of decreased doses.
authors: Waliul Islam, Haiming Chen, Ling Li, Kevan J. Salimian, Florin M. Selaru

10.1126/sciadv.aed4003.title: Learning by moving: Physical motion accelerates category learning
10.1126/sciadv.aed4003.abstract: Categorization is crucial for survival, helping animals forage, navigate, and avoid predators-all tasks involving movement. Yet, dominant theories of category learning treat it as a purely cognitive or perceptual process. Here, we challenge this view by demonstrating that physical movement can enhance category learning-but selectively. Using immersive virtual reality, we found that performing large actions, such as swinging a lightsaber, substantially improved learning of categories requiring integration of multiple cues (e.g., distinguishing aggressive from noncancerous lesions), while having minimal impact on categories involving independent evaluation of features (e.g., sorting by color and shape). This selective enhancement reveals a previously unrecognized motor contribution to categorization and may explain why prior studies missed it, opening avenues for optimizing training in critical categorization tasks.
authors: Luke Rosedahl, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe

10.1126/sciadv.aed6757.title: Polycomb factor PHF19 affects AML initiation, patient prognosis, and survival
10.1126/sciadv.aed6757.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is marked by unchecked expansion of undifferentiated myeloid cells. Although oncogenic fusions such as MLL-AF9 can initiate disease, the early steps of leukemogenesis and the role of cell-intrinsic regulators remain unclear. We previously showed that the Polycomb-associated factor Phf19 is required for hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) maintenance and state control in mice and that its loss (Phf19 KO ) impairs HSC function. To define Phf19’s role in transformation, we expressed MLL-AF9 in Phf19 KO hematopoietic cells and performed integrated multiomic analyses. Phf19 deletion promoted acquisition of stemlike features and reduced responsiveness to differentiation-inducing AML therapies. Molecular and functional consequences of Phf19 loss paralleled those observed in the datasets of patients with AML. From these data, we derived a prognostic signature-PHFScore-which reveals previously unrecognized AML survival-correlating genes that robustly stratify patients across distinct cellular origins and leukemogenic stages, underscoring Phf19’s key role in AML biology and prognosis.
authors: Gianni Paolo Gamarra Figueroa, Arantxa Gutierrez, Enrique Blanco, Pedro Vizán, Cecilia Ballaré, Aleksandra Sparavier, Marta Tosto, Saverio Minucci, Lars Velten, Luciano Di Croce

10.1126/sciadv.aef3338.title: NAD+ metabolic restoration resolves the inflammation-immunocompetence trade-off in lung graft-versus-host disease
10.1126/sciadv.aef3338.abstract: Chronic lung graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) remains difficult to treat, and broad immunosuppression increases infection risk. Single-cell profiling of bronchoalveolar lavage from bronchiolitis obliterans lesions revealed collapse of an epithelial nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) metabolic axis with pathogenic immune-epithelial remodeling, nominating NAD + restoration as an entry point. Because free NAD + is poorly cell-permeable and rapidly consumed, we engineered CaNAD + -PGB-LiP (CNAPL), a high-payload NAD + nanomedicine enabling direct intracellular replenishment. In murine allo-HSCT GVHD, CNAPL improved clinical scores and survival, reduced vascular and epithelial injury, and curtailed hyperinflammation and effector overactivation across GVHD target organs. Unlike immunosuppression, CNAPL preserved phagocytosis, NK/NKT cell (natural killer/natural killer T cell) cytotoxicity, and T cell memory. In posttransplant influenza or Klebsiella infection, CNAPL maintained pathogen control without rekindling GVHD, decoupling inflammation control from infection susceptibility. This metabolism-centered, host-directed strategy restores immune-tissue homeostasis and provides a practical translational path for durable lung GVHD control with preserved antimicrobial defense.

10.1126/sciadv.aei1892.title: Neural circuitry mediating hypercapnia-induced microarousal and impaired sleep depth
10.1126/sciadv.aei1892.abstract: Sleep disruption in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome is characterized by frequent microarousals and reduced sleep depth, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that intermittent hypercapnic air (HA) induces time-locked microarousals, fragments sleep, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep depth, and diminishes rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. HA exposure activates glutamatergic neurons in the nucleus tract solitary (NTS Vglut2 ), and their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is sufficient to trigger arousal and impair sleep. Projection-specific activation reveals that NTS Vglut2 projections to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), parabrachial nucleus (PB), paraventricular thalamus, and locus coeruleus (LC) promote arousal, whereas projections to the PB and LC additionally reduce NREM sleep depth. Inhibition of NTS Vglut2 projection to the PVN significantly postpones HA-induced arousal. NTS Vglut2 terminals monosynaptically activate corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the PVN (PVN CRH ), and inhibition of PVN CRH neurons or knockdown of Slc17a6 (encoding Vglut2), but not Crh , delays hypercapnia-induced arousal. These findings identify neural circuits underlying hypercapnia-induced microarousal and reduced sleep depth.
