10.1126/sciadv.aei0410.title: Pancreatic α cells function as MHC class II-dependent antigen-presenting cells in type 1 diabetes
10.1126/sciadv.aei0410.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by T cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, in which antigen presentation is essential. Although professional antigen-presenting cells initiate autoreactive T cell responses, whether endocrine cells contribute to antigen presentation within inflamed islets remains unclear. Here, we show that pancreatic α cells acquire major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II (MHC-II)-dependent antigen-presenting capacity during T1D progression. Reanalysis of single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from nonobese diabetic (NOD) mice and human T1D islets revealed progressive up-regulation of MHC-II associated genes in α cells. Immunostaining validated the increased of MHC-II level both in NOD mice and patients with T1D. Mechanistically, inflammatory cytokines activated the Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway in α cells, leading to JAK-STAT-dependent MHC-II induction. Functionally, activated α cells internalized, processed, and presented exogenous antigens, acquired expression of costimulatory molecules, and promoted antigen-specific CD4 + T cell activation. These findings identify pancreatic α cells as nonprofessional antigen-presenting cells and expand the current understanding of antigen presentation in autoimmune diabetes.
authors: Zhehui Li, Xinyun Wu, Shuqian Ma, Qingfan Zeng, Xin Wang, Qianyi Xi, Quan-wen Jin, Zuliang Jie, F. Susan Wong, Mingyu Li

10.1126/sciadv.aei1146.title: Rapid, voxel-based 3D printing with yield-stress fluid inks
10.1126/sciadv.aei1146.abstract: Despite decades of progress, 3D printing still presents trade-offs in what materials can be printed and at what resolutions, speeds, and part volumes. We introduce direct ink additive lithography, or DIAL, to alleviate these trade-offs when printing with yield-stress, complex fluid inks used to print functional materials. DIAL combines translational photopatterning with ink sheet deposition for rapid, voxel-based 3D printing. Using model DIAL inks with kilopascal-scale yield stresses, we evaluate how ink rheology influences printing and compare DIAL against digital light processing (DLP) and direct ink writing (DIW). Since DIAL enables fast, high-throughput, support-free, and large-area printing, we showcase its broad potential for producing functional materials by printing multiscale architected, multimaterial, structural electrolyte, and hydrogel structures that are difficult if not impossible to 3D print today.
authors: Pranav Kaarthik, Michael E. Bayer, EunBi Oh, Alexander Q. Kane, Ryan L. Truby

10.1126/sciadv.aei1795.title: A biofilm-derived peptide as an underwater adhesive
10.1126/sciadv.aei1795.abstract: Wet adhesives that perform under water have broad applications in industrial and biomedical settings. To date, molecular designs for underwater adhesives have largely been inspired by marine animals including mussels and barnacles. Here, we propose bacterial biofilms as an alternative source of inspiration for underwater adhesives. Specifically, we demonstrate the application potential of a peptide derived from biofilms formed by the notorious pathogen Vibrio cholerae . We characterize the ability of this biofilm-derived peptide to adsorb onto various surfaces and to glue wet surfaces by using a combination of confocal microscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, atomic force microscopy, lap shear tests, and spectroscopic tools. We further show that the peptide can coaggregate with microspheres acting as an effective flocculant. Our results open new design possibilities for underwater adhesives inspired by natural biofilms.
authors: Xin Huang, Ewelina D. Liszczyk, Ramesh Prasad, Megan E. Mitchell, Zhijie Wang, Yuchu Liu, Sarvagya Saluja, Mingyu Wang, Rebekah A. Jackson, Peter Dahl, Roberto Andresen Eguiluz, Nikhil Malvankar, Elsa C. Y. Yan, Rich Olson, Huan-Xiang Zhou, Jing Yan

10.1126/sciadv.aei1954.title: A high robustness decoding technique for ultrasound modulated electroencephalogram
10.1126/sciadv.aei1954.abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. However, under extremely complex scenarios, excessively strong or weak acoustoelectric signal coupling leads to severe distortion in USMEEG decoded signals. To address this, we developed a highly robust decoding algorithm based on the ultrasound pulse repetition frequency and introduced the acoustoelectric modulation ratio (AMR) to quantify different modulation scenarios. Across numerical simulations, phantoms, and validation using human steady-state visual evoked potential signals with data-level acoustoelectric coupling across 10 volunteers, the focused ultrasound phased array achieved an encoding spatial resolution of 0.79 millimeters. The proposed algorithm significantly outperformed four traditional methods, exhibiting higher precision under weak modulation (0 < AMR ≤ 0.6), moderate modulation (0.6 < AMR ≤ 1), and over modulation (AMR > 1) conditions, with average decoding correlations reaching 0.84, 0.90, and 0.89. This highly robust technique expands USMEEG applications and provides a technical foundation for high-performance noninvasive brain-computer interfaces.
authors: Xue Wang, Guowei Chen, Jia He, Pu Wang, Rongxu Guo, Shenjie Ji, Mingyu Li, Feng He, Yanqiu Zhang, Xiqi Jian, Hao Zhang, Minpeng Xu, Dong Ming

10.1126/sciadv.aei5129.title: Effector-triggered stomatal immunity prevents leaf invasion by bacterial pathogens
10.1126/sciadv.aei5129.abstract: The phytopathogen Pseudomonas syringae must enter the leaf interior through natural openings such as stomata to cause disease. Plants restrict pathogen entry into the leaf through non-self-recognition-driven stomatal closure. P. syringae counters this stomatal immunity by deploying a range of toxins and effectors. Here, we show that stomatal immunity in Arabidopsis thaliana is reinforced upon recognition of the ubiquitous P. syringae type III effector AvrE1 by the resistance protein CAR1. CAR1 expression is enriched in guard cells, and its activation prolongs the effective duration of stomatal immunity. We also show that CAR1 prevents the invasion of leaf tissue by natural isolates of P. syringae , demonstrating that stomatal immunity provides a broadly significant barrier to host accessibility by P. syringae that carry the conserved effector AvrE1.
authors: Tamar V. Av-Shalom, Yan Lai, Racquel A. Singh, Dora Yuping Wang, Reid Gohmann, David Mackey, Darrell Desveaux, David S. Guttman

10.1126/sciadv.aei5545.title: Dynamic redox reactivation of platinum sites for long-term glycolate electrosynthesis from polyethylene terephthalate wastes
10.1126/sciadv.aei5545.abstract: Glycolates are indispensable in the health, chemical and pharmaceutical industries, whereas their mainstream production involve toxic chemicals and harsh operating condition. An alternative route for glycolate production is electrifying ethylene glycol (EG) that originates from polyethylene terephthalate (PET) but suffers from poor durability of active platinum site that tend to deactivate. Herein, we demonstrate a dynamic redox reactivation strategy, which alternates between working potential for oxidizing EG to glycolate and nonworking potential for reviving active platinum sites by the chemical reduction of adsorbed EG, realizing an unprecedented stability for over 3000 hours under average current density of ∼220 milliamperes per square centimeter. Upscaling this approach, the assembled electrolyzer drives a record current of 10 amperes at 1.18 volts for repeatable 40 batches of glycolates electrosynthesis, with each batch converting 48.0 grams of PET to 11.6 grams of glycolates (52.8% yield), 37.7 grams of p -phthalic acid (95.8% yield), 248.7 grams of NaHSO 4 (95.2% yield) and ∼11.5 liters of hydrogen, showcasing a considerable revenue of ∼$1072 per ton glycolate.
authors: Zehao Xiao, Hongyu Guo, Yu Gu, Changze Wei, Zheng Lin, Mingchuan Luo, Shaojun Guo

10.1126/sciadv.aei7819.title: Massively parallel self-assembly of suspendable microcompartments for functional cell screening
10.1126/sciadv.aei7819.abstract: Modern biology increasingly demands platforms that can compartmentalize and analyze single cells and cell-cell interactions at massive scale, yet existing compartmentalization strategies based on microfluidics suffer from critical limitations. Emerging lab-on-a-particle technologies such as nanovials enable anchored single cells or small groups of cells to be isolated and assayed in a fully suspendable and parallelized manner using standard instrumentation, although their open architectures can result in loss of growing or un-attached cells. Here, we introduce capped nanovials: self-assembling hydrogel compartments formed by docking spherical capping particles into bowl-shaped nanovials. We routinely achieve capping of >80% of all nanovials in a sample and >90% sorting yield by flow cytometry, making the capped nanovial system well-suited for preparing and running large-scale assays. Furthermore, we demonstrate stable clonal expansion of single mammalian, yeast, and bacterial cells; growth-based selections of >10,000 colonies; enhanced signal-to-noise in secretion assays; and high-purity selection of antibody-secreting cells based on activation of co-encapsulated T cell reporters (>30-fold signal, up to 100% selection purity). By combining the simplicity of a well plate with the functional precision of droplet microfluidics without requiring oil or custom instrumentation, capped nanovials realize accessible, high-throughput, and high-resolution experimentation.
authors: Michael Mellody, Yuta Nakagawa, Alyssa Arnheim, Lily Shang, Catherine Soo, Natalie Tsubamoto, Sarah Taylor, Rajesh Ghosh, Megan Ho, Anna-Marie Guenther, Sumedha Shastry, Wesley Luk, Ian Morales, Jesse Liang, Joseph de Rutte, Richard G. James, Dino Di Carlo

10.1126/sciadv.aei7948.title: Human carotid plaque risk imaging using multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound fusion (hCAPRI)
10.1126/sciadv.aei7948.abstract: Assessing the risk of carotid plaque rupture remains limited because current imaging methods cannot provide both plaque composition and structural information in real time. Here, we present human carotid plaque risk imaging (hCAPRI), a multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound (PA/US) fusion method for real-time carotid plaque assessment. hCAPRI combines PA imaging for detecting intraplaque hemorrhage (IPH) with US imaging for evaluating the plaque structure. PA imaging measured IPH size and methemoglobin content, while US imaging assessed stenosis severity, calcification, and plaque thickness. Combining these PA/US parameters, we compute an hCAPRI score. In 171 carotid arteries (CAs) from 120 patients, hCAPRI revealed the relationships among the PA/US parameters. In 36 CAs validated with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), hCAPRI showed high agreement with MRI. The hCAPRI score achieved 89% sensitivity and 84% specificity for high-risk plaque classification. hCAPRI offers a low-cost, real-time, and contrast-free approach for carotid plaque risk imaging.
authors: Minsik Sung, Sunghun Nam, Sun Oh Kim, Jong-il Park, Dong Young Jeong, Yujung Jung, Changyeop Lee, Moongyu Han, Hong-Ju Kim, Jun-Chang Jeong, Kwanju Song, Jeong Yoon Song, Jae Young Park, Hyeseon Lee, Bum Joon Kim, Byullee Park, Ung Kim, Chulhong Kim

10.1126/sciadv.aej0686.title: Lighting up necrotic neurons from traumatic brain injury with magnetic quantum dots to decode the cellular origin of MRI
10.1126/sciadv.aej0686.abstract: The diagnosis of traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains heavily constrained by the limitations of conventional imaging techniques in visualizing the pathological events that determine the disease progression and outcome. To address this clinical challenge, we report a manganese-doped near-infrared quantum dot (QD) to intrinsically integrate the highly sensitive optical imaging with clinical compatible magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Taking the advantages of optical imaging powered by whole-brain clearing and cellular resolution three-dimensional (3D) panoptic imaging, in combination with the systematic in vitro cell studies on different types of cells involved in TBI, we disclosed the interpretable pathology reflected by TBI imaging through the highly sensitive fluorescence of magnetic QDs, i.e., after systemic administration, the nanoprobes were extravasated through the compromised blood-brain barrier and then selectively phagocytosed by activated microglia, which subsequently migrated into the regions rich in dead neurons and neuronal debris. This microglia-mediated tropism decodes the signal origin of MRI enhanced by the nanometer-sized contrast agent, thereby transforming the MRI from an anatomical tool into a pathological reporter. A biocompatible Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticle of similar size was also compared with the magnetic QD mentioned above for validating the translational merits of nanoparticles in MRI diagnosis of TBI.
authors: Mingxia Jiao, Xin Zhao, Jingyun Wang, Wanru Tian, Yao Li, Xuan Cheng, Kun Zhang, Xiliang Luo, Peisen Zhang, Mingyuan Gao

10.1126/sciadv.aej0867.title: Mechano-electrochemical energy harvesting and self-powered sensing via dynamic liquid metal-electrolyte interfaces
10.1126/sciadv.aej0867.abstract: Wearable devices, stretchable sensors, and soft electronics benefit from harvesting ambient energy using compliant materials, yet existing approaches often face limitations in power density, scalability, and electrode adaptability. Here, we report a liquid metal mechano-electrochemical energy harvester (LMMEEH) that converts mechanical stimuli into electricity through dynamically regulated electrode-electrolyte interfaces. Mechanical motion changes the interfacial area and drives asymmetric Faradaic reactions associated with dynamic oxide formation and dissolution, generating electrical output. The fluidity, high surface tension, and self-renewing surface chemistry of liquid metals enable rapid interfacial reformation, large reversible deformation, and stable cyclic operation. The device achieves a power density of 140.2 microwatts per square meter and scales to a 40-unit array producing 2 volts. Spatial and temporal programming of the liquid metal interfaces further enables synchronized three-phase alternating-current generation. We demonstrate wave-driven emergency lighting, self-powered pressure sensing, and real-time physiological monitoring. This work establishes dynamic liquid metal electrochemical interfaces as a scalable strategy for soft mechanical energy harvesting and self-powered electronics.
authors: Xiangbo Zhou, Hongda Lu, Jialu Wang, Yipu Guo, Liping Gong, Jian Shu, Zhisheng Lv, Haiping Du, Shiwu Zhang, Michael D. Dickey, Weihua Li

10.1126/sciadv.aej0978.title: Rapid activation kinetics of the NLR Swordholder underpin nonhost resistance to Phytophthora capsici in Nicotiana tabacum
10.1126/sciadv.aej0978.abstract: Nonhost resistance (NHR) represents a durable phenomenon where plants resist nonadapted pathogens. While NHR holds substantial potential for engineering crops with broad-spectrum and durable resistance, its underlying molecular mechanism remains incompletely understood. The oomycete pathogen Phytophthora capsici is nonadapted to Nicotiana tabacum (Nt) but is virulent on the closely related Nicotiana benthamiana (Nb). Here, we demonstrated that both species encode the NLR Swordholder (Swh), which recognizes P. capsici AvrNt effector proteins. NtSwh restores NHR in ntswh mutants, whereas NbSwh confers only partial resistance. Mechanistically, NtSwh exhibits weaker autoinhibition mediated by its amino-terminal extension domains, enabling rapid immune signaling that prevent pathogen effector-mediated suppression; NbSwh’s stronger autoinhibition delays activation, permitting effector suppression. Heterologous expression of NtSwh in tomato enhances field resistance to P. capsici without yield penalty. These findings indicate that the kinetics of NLR can play a key role in defining NHR, in addition to the presence or absence of specific NLRs, providing insights into strategies for breeding durable crop immunity.
authors: Xiaowei Fu, Xianglan Li, Wenyi Zhu, Yueyi Ren, Tianli Li, Chuyan Xia, Xiaohua Dong, Zhaojie Chen, Jinding Liu, Danyu Shen, Li Wan, Gan Ai, Daolong Dou

10.1126/sciadv.aek6976.title: Direct regulation of a tRNA modification enzyme by ppGpp links stress signaling to translational control and biofilm development
10.1126/sciadv.aek6976.abstract: Transfer RNA (tRNA) modifications influence decoding efficiency and translational fidelity, yet how they are integrated into bacterial signaling networks remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a direct connection between stress signaling and codon-specific translational regulation. We show that the alarmone guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) directly inhibits MnmE (TrmE), a conserved tRNA-modification GTPase required for methylaminomethyl (mnm) modification of wobble uridine. High-resolution ribosome profiling in Bacillus subtilis revealed that loss of MnmE selectively increases ribosome pausing at AAG codons and reprograms translation of a subset of genes, including small open reading frames. Among these is a previously unrecognized AAG-containing leader peptide that controls expression of the biofilm repressor AbrB. Consistent with this mechanism, mnmE mutants exhibit constitutive extracellular matrix production and bypass the biofilm defect of a relA mutant. Together, these findings establish a pathway linking ppGpp signaling, tRNA modification, codon-specific translation, and multicellular development.
authors: Aude E. Trinquier, Franck Slama, Junlang Liu, Lucille Pham, Lauren Stolt, Jue D. Wang

10.1126/sciadv.aeh5390.title: A disynaptic trigeminal circuit for the transformation and integration of oral chemesthesis in male mice
10.1126/sciadv.aeh5390.abstract: Chemesthesis, encompassing oral sensations such as spiciness and coolness, is an important yet incompletely understood component of mammalian chemical sensing. Unlike taste or olfaction, these sensations are conveyed primarily through trigeminal pathways; however, how modality-specific peripheral signals are processed and transformed along central ascending pathways remains poorly understood. Herein, we delineate the structural and functional organization of an ascending trigeminal-brainstem-parabrachial circuit that mediates oral chemesthetic processing in male mice. Using viral tracing, in vivo calcium imaging, and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, we identify a genetically defined disynaptic glutamatergic pathway (trigeminal ganglion → spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis → lateral parabrachial nucleus) that is both necessary and sufficient for capsaicin- and menthol-evoked defensive behaviors. Although peripheral TRPV1 + and TRPM8 + neurons retain a degree of modality bias, we observe substantial convergence of spicy and cooling signals within the spinal trigeminal nucleus, followed by sustained and synchronized population activity in vglut2 + neurons of the external lateral parabrachial nucleus. This hierarchical transformation from peripheral segregation to central integration reveals the organizational principle by which distinct chemesthetic modalities are progressively integrated along a trigeminal-mediated ascending pathway, providing a circuit-level framework for understanding how chemical stimuli are processed and coordinated to drive defensive behaviors.

10.1126/sciadv.aef6880.title: On-virion structural dynamics reveal temperature- and receptor-coordinated activation of an alphacoronavirus spike
authors: Jiaming Liang, Cheng Peng, Ruixiao Tan, Yutong Song, Zheyuan Zhang, Jinfang Yu, Xinquan Wang, Sai Li

10.1126/sciadv.aeb0364.title: Oxygen fugacity, temperature, and pressure of Siberian eclogitic diamonds: Implications for the Archaean convecting mantle redox state
10.1126/sciadv.aeb0364.abstract: Kimberlite-borne eclogite xenoliths ultimately derive from ancient subducted oceanic crust. Some specimens still record the chemical and redox conditions of their igneous protoliths, allowing a view into contemporaneous convecting mantle sources. However, accurate reconstructions are limited because eclogites have been exposed to metasomatism in the subcontinental mantle for billions of years. Here, we investigated garnet and clinopyroxene inclusions, both touching and nontouching pairs, in 19 eclogitic diamonds from the Siberian craton, hence shielded from post-entrapment overprint. Inclusion compositions indicate average sampling depths of 180 to 280 km, temperatures of 1030° to 1540°C (±60°C), and redox conditions, for most of the samples, oxidized enough for diamonds to have originated from water(carbonate)-rich fluids. The reconstructed bulk composition points to basaltic oceanic crust formed from an Archaean convecting mantle region that was more oxygen-depleted than today, providing compelling evidence of redox heterogeneities in the source rocks of ancient oceanic crust.
authors: Giulia Marras, Denis Mikhailenko, Catherine A. McCammon, Sonja Aulbach, Yuhang Lu, Renbiao Tao, Alla Logvinova, Dmitry Zedgenizov, Vincenzo Stagno

10.1126/sciadv.aek8532.title: Accumulated radicals by GHz femtosecond burst drive one-step superhydrophobic conversion
10.1126/sciadv.aek8532.abstract: Short-lived radicals usually decay before they can drive long-range reactions, making laser-induced radical chain reactions difficult to sustain. Here, we used GHz femtosecond bursts to temporally couple excitation events, allowing reactive intermediates from preceding subpulses to remain available for subsequent reactions and favoring their transient accumulation relative to isolated-pulse excitation. Consistent with this temporally coupled process, the methylphenyl silicone resin/graphene/CuFe 2 O 4 /SiO 2 composite coating exhibits a threshold-like nonlinear wettability transition near 430 subpulses. Compared with the microsecond-spaced single-pulse femtosecond regime, the sub-nanosecond GHz burst produces more extensive chemical conversion, enabling one-step bond reorganization and phase transformation and yielding a low-adhesion superhydrophobic surface with a contact angle of 161° ± 0.7° without posttreatment. Pulse-timing-controlled radical-mediated chemistry thus provides a time-domain strategy for ultrafast materials synthesis.
authors: Junke Huang, Jiachen Yin, Shupeng Xu, Tao Yuan, Tianjun Yao, Zhen Zhang, Mengyun Hu, Heping Zeng

10.1126/sciadv.aeb4683.title: Defining epidemiologically relevant units of cholera transmission in sub-Saharan Africa
10.1126/sciadv.aeb4683.abstract: Much remains unknown about cholera transmission dynamics in Africa. Applying both traditional phylogeographic techniques and innovative methods for combining epidemiologic and genomic data, we identified three to four distinct “cholera transmission units” within which cross-border cholera transmission has been more frequent. These units can be grouped into two major transmission clusters, one in Western Africa and bordering countries and one spanning the Central, Eastern, and Southern regions. Simulation studies show that these clusters can be used to assess the risk of international spread of introduced cholera strains and identify heterogeneities in the speed of international spread based on outbreak location. Our methods further allow us to infer cholera incidence attributable to specific lineages in the absence of sequencing data. This work has clear implications for cholera control.
authors: Bethany L. DiPrete, Javier Perez-Saez, Shirlee Wohl, Nathaniel Matteson, Seungwon Kim, Andrew S. Azman, Justin Lessler

10.1126/sciadv.aei6340.title: Photoinitiator-free gelatin hydrogel microneedles for acute gouty arthritis treatment
10.1126/sciadv.aei6340.abstract: Photo-crosslinked microneedles (MNs) are widely used in biomedical applications, but their dependence on exogenous photoinitiators continues to pose a fundamental challenge to their further advancement. Herein, we have developed a hydrogel MN system loaded with self-assembled nanoparticles (NPs). The NPs are composed of natural polyphenols and indomethacin. The MN system is rapidly dissolving and is fabricated through an initiator-free photo-crosslinking process. Systematic investigation of the gel composition, swelling behavior, and mechanical properties of lipoic acid-modified gelatin (GelLA)-based MNs demonstrated both swelling and mechanical strength could be readily tuned. Notably, the tunable mechanical feature of GelLA enabled effective penetration of the stratum corneum, facilitating efficient transdermal drug delivery. Compared with gelatin methacryloyl, GelLA-based hydrogel MNs prepared at the same concentration exhibited superior biocompatibility, while eliminating the potential cytotoxicity associated with exogenous photoinitiators. Further in vivo evaluation in an acute gouty arthritis model demonstrated that the MN system could significantly alleviate joint inflammation through rapid drug release, highlighting its potent anti-inflammatory efficacy. Overall, this initiator-free, photo-crosslinkable GelLA-based MNs system offered a safe, efficient, and user-friendly strategy for local drug delivery in the management of acute gouty arthritis.

10.1126/sciadv.aeg8172.title: Beyond the golden rule of polymer network dynamics: Design principles for tissue-mimetic viscoelasticity
10.1126/sciadv.aeg8172.abstract: Technologies ranging from transportation to biomedical devices rely on soft materials whose performance hinges on balancing stiffness and damping. In conventional polymer networks, however, these properties are typically coupled: Softer materials are intrinsically more dissipative, reflecting a long-standing correlation in polymer dynamics that severely restricts the accessible design space. Here, we move beyond this longstanding constraint using brush-like polymer networks whose architecture in combination with chemistry governs viscoelastic response. By independently tuning strand volume and flexibility, we vary the elastic modulus over orders of magnitude while maintaining nearly constant relaxation time without altering network chemistry. Our findings establish a general framework for encoding viscoelastic responses in polymer networks, enabling the design of tissue-mimetic materials with programmable equilibrium stiffness and rate-dependent dissipation.

10.1126/sciadv.aeg0031.title: Modeling the effects of climate risk on primates globally: New perspectives on conservation priorities
10.1126/sciadv.aeg0031.abstract: Rapid climate change poses a severe threat to biodiversity, and phylogenetic diversity-a key metric capturing evolutionary uniqueness and adaptive potential-is critical for conservation. Integrating a well-resolved phylogenetic tree of 424 primate species, we combined spatial analysis and climate risk modeling to explore global spatiotemporal patterns of primates and assess their vulnerability under future climate scenarios. The results suggest a pronounced latitudinal pattern in primate distribution, with isothermality and annual mean precipitation as key drivers. Primate species in the American tropics (Mexico, Central, and South America) and southern China showed later divergence times and lower phylogenetic diversity, emerging as neo-hotspots for primates. Under future climate change, species in these neo-hotspots will face higher climate risks than those in paleo-hotspots of primate diversity. In addition, high human pressure, high climate risk, and limited protected area coverage increase species and population survival risks in hotspot regions. Overall, this global study deepens our understanding of biodiversity conservation under current climate change scenarios and synergistically advances the preservation of numerous natural services essential to ecosystem health and human well-being. Our study provides a spatially explicit framework to fulfill Targets 3 and 8 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

10.1126/sciadv.aei1901.title: Betel nut sucking is the earliest recorded evidence for the habitual use of a neuroactive plant drug
10.1126/sciadv.aei1901.abstract: The modern custom of chewing betel nuts is practiced by around 1 in 10 people worldwide, yet the earliest beginnings of this widespread drug use habit are unknown. We report rare skeletal remains of two preagricultural foragers from Sulawesi (Indonesia), both displaying a dental pathology that we establish was caused by a hitherto unknown precursor to betel chewing: habitual sucking of whole betel nuts. Previous reports suggested that the main neuroactive alkaloid in betel nut, arecoline, is released by masticating the processed nut with slaked lime. However, our experiments demonstrate that simply keeping intact betel nuts in the oral cavity for prolonged periods releases arecoline. Biomolecular analysis of the ancient human teeth is also consistent with this early form of ingesting betel nut. With the earliest forager dating to 25 to 16 thousand years ago, our findings suggest the use of betel nut as a drug has more ancient origins than previously supposed.

10.1126/sciadv.aef2512.title: Bacteriophage PAK_P3 genome structuration and dynamics during infection of Pseudomonas aeruginosa reveal specific interaction patterns
10.1126/sciadv.aef2512.abstract: While the dynamic changes in genome organization in cellular organisms have been well described, the three-dimensional (3D) folding of phage genomes during the infection of their host is extremely limited. Understanding how phage genomes fold, invade, and rearrange the genome of their host to functionally organize the optimal expression of their genes remains unknown. Here, we explore the spatial dynamics of the virulent double-stranded DNA phage PAK_P3 during infection of its host Pseudomonas aeruginosa and reveal how its genome rapidly decondenses to adopt a specific 3D organization that reflects its transcriptional program. Concomitantly, the host genome decondenses as gene expression wanes and transcription-induced domains vanish. We also uncover specific contacts of the phage genome with host chromosome, showing how the phage genome exploits the spatial genome architecture of its host to succeed in its infection cycle. Our data highlight an unprecedented level of genome folding and gene expression regulation during a viral infection.

10.1126/sciadv.aec4911.title: Dendritic shaft constrictions shape synaptic integration in neurons
10.1126/sciadv.aec4911.abstract: For nearly 150 years, textbooks have described dendritic morphology as optimized for efficient synaptic voltage transfer from spines to the soma, implemented as a tubular design respecting Rall’s 3/2 rule for impedance matching at branch points. Here, we reveal that this view is an oversimplification. Using multiple high-resolution imaging techniques, we demonstrate that dendrites in cortical and hippocampal neurons exhibit nanoscale constrictions, termed dendritic shaft constrictions (DSCs), with diameters ranging from ∼100 to 500 nanometers in mice. We also identified DSCs in human hippocampal and cortical neurons. We provide theoretical and experimental lines of evidence that these constrictions effectively partition the dendrite into distinct electrical compartments, shaping dendritic integration of synaptic potentials.

10.1126/sciadv.aec5478.title: Reconstructing pathogen-specific antibody binding epitopes and age-dependent immune signatures from proteomic-scale peptide libraries
10.1126/sciadv.aec5478.abstract: High-density peptide arrays are useful for mapping linear antibody epitopes and resolution of antibody specificity in a single-assay platform. Here, we used peptide library screening to evaluate magnitude and breadth of humoral responses to enteric pathogens in the context of public health interventions. We characterized the epitope landscape to known immunogenic proteins to several viruses, bacteria, and parasites and used that to infer immunological profiles at age 3, 14, and 28 months. The peptide libraries detected immune signatures better for viruses compared with bacteria and parasites and captured distinct dynamics of protein-level variation in immune signatures over time. We found limited sensitivity for bacterial and protozoan pathogens whose humoral responses may depend more on conformational or natively modified epitopes than linear-peptide binding. Unbiased peptide libraries have potential utility for broad analysis of antibody responses in integrated serosurveillance, but our results reveal pathogen-specific limitations where peptide-based serology would be less predictive of true infection status and where it would provide greater surveillance value. Beyond assay performance, peptide arrays are useful for studying epitope architecture, and a practical implication would require augmentation with alternative antigen formats (whole-protein or folded antigens) in a complementary hybrid approach.

10.1126/sciadv.aec3842.title: Myasthenia thymus reprograms class-switched B cells into BAFF-dependent survivors
10.1126/sciadv.aec3842.abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) presents a clinical challenge where autoantibody titers poorly predict disease severity, and thymectomy provides inconsistent benefits. We hypothesized that thymic B cells acquire survival mechanisms that bypass canonical tolerance checkpoints, enabling persistence independent of antigen-specific selection. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, V(D)J repertoire analysis, and spatial transcriptomics to generate the largest MG atlas to date (237,661 cells), we identified a tolerance checkpoint swap in MG pathogenesis. Pathological class-switched B cells within thymic germinal centers exhibited reduced antigen presentation ( CD74 and CD1C ) and diminished CD40 costimulation while up-regulating TNFRSF17 to engage BAFF-driven survival. This shift allows polyclonal autoreactive B cells to evade stringent selection and seed peripheral sites. T follicular helper cells supported this reprogramming via increased TNFSF13B and CHGB expression, with the latter facilitating dopamine-mediated synaptic acceleration. These findings offer insight into clinical paradoxes in MG and point to the BAFF-BCMA axis as a potential therapeutic target and biomarkers for disease activity.

10.1126/sciadv.adw6168.title: Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
10.1126/sciadv.adw6168.abstract: Many terrestrial insects transition from humid to dry environments at metamorphosis, yet how they avoid dehydration is unclear. In Drosophila melanogaster , we identify a lipid barrier to water loss in the pupa that is anatomically distinct from that of the adult. It comprises unisex hydrocarbons that are longer and less volatile than their sex-specific adult counterparts. These hyperlong hydrocarbons are produced by larval oenocytes and stored in the fat body for subsequent transport to the cuticle at pupariation. A fatty acid elongase, EloHL, is required for hyperlong hydrocarbon biosynthesis and for a functional barrier to dehydration during early metamorphosis. Hyperlong barrier hydrocarbons are widespread across the Drosophila genus and typically transition to shorter sex-specific versions during adult maturation. In the desert species D. mojavensis , however, adults retain hyperlong hydrocarbons. This study reveals how insect lipid barriers are tuned to environmental variations in aridity and temperature during development and evolution.
authors: Lena Lampe, Clare L. Newell, Bing-Jun Wang, Andrew P. Bailey, Rami Makki, Cyrille Alexandre, Ian S. Gilmore, Li Zhao, Alex P. Gould

10.1126/sciadv.aea3106.title: Brainstem enkephalinergic neural circuit underlying cold-induced pain relief in mice
10.1126/sciadv.aea3106.abstract: Application of cold or cold-mimicking chemicals to injury has long been recognized as an effective means of pain relief. However, underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified a cold-responsive neuronal subset within the lateral parabrachial nucleus (lPBN), the thermosensory relay region in the hindbrain, that mediates cold-induced analgesia in mice. Activation of these neurons and their projection to ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) increased the nociceptive threshold, while ablation of these neurons attenuated analgesia induced by cold-mimicking chemicals. We further identified that these neurons express precursor gene of enkephalin ( Penk ), which is necessary for TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8)-mediated pain relief. Mechanistically, cold-responsive lPBN neurons frequency-dependently released enkephalin peptide into vlPAG to activate the descending pain modulation circuitry via disinhibition. Activation of cold-responsive neurons reduced spinal cord responses to noxious stimuli, suggesting the involvement of a top-down pain modulation pathway. These findings propose a central mechanism underlying cold-induced pain relief, which could be a novel therapeutic target.
authors: Hayun Kim, Yoonkyung Lee, Seog Bae Oh

10.1126/sciadv.aeb8568.title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
10.1126/sciadv.aeb8568.abstract: Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Double-negative regulatory T cells (DNTreg) are important immune regulatory cells that maintain liver immune homeostasis. However, their survival and function are compromised in MASLD. Herein, we found that mevalonate pathway and its rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) were significantly down-regulated in DNTreg from both mice and patients with MASLD, correlating with impaired DNTreg viability and immunosuppressive function. Arachidonic acid is enriched in MASLD liver and inhibits DNTreg HMGCR expression. Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), a downstream product of HMGCR, mediates RAC1 geranylgeranylation, which facilitates its interaction with mitochondrial CLPX protease, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and immunoregulatory activity of DNTreg. Adoptive transfer of Pggt1b +/− DNTreg into MASLD mice demonstrated significantly diminished therapeutic efficacy compared with wild-type DNTreg. In conclusion, mevalonate metabolism-mediated geranylgeranylation is essential for the suppressive activity and immune homeostasis of DNTreg in MASLD.
authors: Hua Jin, Xiyu Wang, Longyang Zhou, Xinjie Zhong, Yunxiong Wei, Xiaotong Han, Nan Xu, Peiyang Fang, Zihan Zhang, Xiaonan Du, Mengyi Li, Songlin Wang, Zhongtao Zhang, Guangyong Sun, Dong Zhang

10.1126/sciadv.aec4195.title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
10.1126/sciadv.aec4195.abstract: Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, with CD4 + cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.
authors: Andrew G. T. Pyo, Adlina Chan, Joshua Rosenheim, Clare Thakker, Lucy Bell, Gayathri Nageswaran, Suzanne Byrne, Ben Killingley, David Scobie, Mariya Kalinova, Alison Boyers, Andrew Catchpole, Alex Mann, Rik G. H. 10.1126/sciadv.aee1766.title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
10.1126/sciadv.aee1766.abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.
authors: Fia B. Larsen, Vasileios Voutsinos, Nicolas Jonsson, Kristoffer E. Johansson, Freia D. Ethelberg, Isa K. Henrichs, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen, Rasmus Hartmann-Petersen

10.1126/sciadv.aee4682.title: Shape-memory scaffold targets inflammation and fibrosis to restore endometrium and fertility in intrauterine adhesions
10.1126/sciadv.aee4682.abstract: Intrauterine adhesion (IUA) is a major cause of infertility, yet current treatments remain limited in preventing fibrosis and restoring functional endometrium. We report a bi-drug, bifunctional, biodegradable shape-memory regenerative (BiSMR) scaffold enabling minimally invasive implantation, sequential drug release, and barrier protection. Proteomic profiling of chemical, mechanical, and combined injury models revealed inflammatory activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired regenerative programs, providing a molecular rationale for combining epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) with 17β-estradiol (E 2 ). BiSMR couples an E 2 -loaded PLTG [poly( l -lactide)- co -trimethylene carbonate- co -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E 2 delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.
authors: Keyi Yang, Haoming Wu, Teng Ma, Yao Zhang, Jiayu Liu, Yingying Chen, Mei Liu, Qiong Wu, Shuhao Yang, Yao Wang, Wanyue Feng, Xin Yong, Xulin Hu, Huili Zhu

10.1126/sciadv.aee6434.title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
10.1126/sciadv.aee6434.abstract: Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10 −7 hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.
authors: Joel K. Jose, Andrea Marchese, Marion Cromb, Hendrik Ulbricht, Andrejs Cebers, Ping Koy Lam, Tao Wang, Andrea Vinante

10.1126/sciadv.aee7761.title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
10.1126/sciadv.aee7761.abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger-activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state-adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.
authors: Yongjin Hu, Jiabo Li, Guixian Wang, Xiao Wang, Zhiyuan Zhu, Jingyi Rao

10.1126/sciadv.aee9459.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
10.1126/sciadv.aee9459.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.
authors: Layla A. Schuster, Beibei Liu, Jose Cleydson F. Silva, Xi Cheng, Raquel Dias, Meixia Zhao

10.1126/sciadv.aef6604.title: A robust spin-coupled tetraradical via nonalternant design
10.1126/sciadv.aef6604.abstract: Polyradicals in open-shell polycyclic hydrocarbons (PHs) offer access to multiple spin states and hold great promise for spintronics and quantum technologies. Here we report a nonalternant, air-stable tetraradical featuring two fused 7-5-7 rings and a strongly correlated singlet ground state. This molecule displays an exceptional tetraradical character ( y 0 = 1.00, y 1 = 0.89) and exhibits long ambient stability ( t 1/2 = 33 days). Comprehensive electronic structure and magnetic response analyses reveal that the spin topology is governed by both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, with robust electron correlation ( J 1 = +321 K, J 2 = −44 K, and J 3 = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness-key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.
authors: Weixiang Zhou, Yu-Shuang Zhang, Gaetano Ricci, Yubin Fu, David Casanova, Juan Casado, Shang-Da Jiang, Junzhi Liu

10.1126/sciadv.aeg5123.title: Spatial proteomics reveals lipid droplet reorganization in symbiotic Paramecium bursaria cells
10.1126/sciadv.aeg5123.abstract: Endosymbiosis is an important adaptive mechanism allowing organisms to exploit previously inaccessible niches. The flexible relationship between the ciliate Paramecium bursaria and green algae represents a model system for studying early endosymbiosis evolution. However, the mechanisms underlying how P. bursaria cells maintain this endosymbiotic relationship remain unclear. Here, we use mass spectrometry-based proteomics to generate a spatial proteomic atlas of the host P. bursaria cells with and without endosymbionts. This atlas defines the protein composition of the endosymbiont-containing compartment (perialgal vacuole) and reveals pronounced remodeling of host lipid droplets upon symbiosis. Imaging analyses confirm that lipid droplets change in size, morphology, and positioning, accumulating near intracellular algae. Perturbing symbiotic cells with chemical inhibitors of lipid metabolism reduces endosymbiotic algal numbers, revealing a role for lipid droplets in the host-endosymbiont interaction. Our data provide a comprehensive resource for protein localization in P. bursaria cells and elucidate how those cells remodel an existing cellular compartment to maintain endosymbiosis.
authors: Yan-Jun Chen, Md Mostafa Kamal, Chuan-Chih Hsu, Jun-Yi Leu

10.1126/sciadv.aeg5924.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux
10.1126/sciadv.aeg5924.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.
authors: So-Hee Son, Sangwon Bae, Soo Young Moon, Minhye Kim, Seung Soo Oh, Chang Yun Son, Ju Young Lee

10.1126/sciadv.aeg8175.title: Visualizing nanoscopic acoustic mode competition in a van der Waals ferroelectric
10.1126/sciadv.aeg8175.abstract: Understanding how low-dimensional ferroelectrics respond to ultrafast excitation at nanoscales is essential for controlling energy flow and mechanical functionality in next-generation polar devices, yet the nanoscopic structural response to ultrafast depolarization remains unresolved, obscuring the microscopic pathways of acoustic decoherence and energy dissipation. Here, we spatiotemporally resolve lattice motion in the van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI 2 using combined ultrafast electron microscopy and diffraction, revealing three acoustic phonons: two transverse shear modes and one longitudinal breathing mode. The transverse mode that shears the layers perpendicular to the in-plane polar axis dominates over that along the polar axis, reflecting anisotropic polarization-strain coupling. Real-space mapping uncovers spatially correlated heterogeneity in mode amplitudes and lifetimes. Regions dominated by a single shear mode exhibit significantly longer acoustic lifetimes than multimode regions, suggesting acoustic phonon-phonon scattering as a major source of decoherence. Our results provide a microscopic understanding of ultrafast depolarization-driven acoustic dynamics and spatially heterogeneous energy dissipation in van der Waals ferroelectrics.
authors: Zhaodong Chu, Carter Fox, Zixin Zhai, Suman Kumari, Haihua Liu, Priti Yadav, Yue Li, Bing Lv, Thomas E. Gage, Jun Xiao, Haidan Wen

10.1126/sciadv.aeh0938.title: Scaling up chemical recycling: High-yield polyolefin pyrolysis to liquid hydrocarbons using iron single atom catalysts
10.1126/sciadv.aeh0938.abstract: The chemical recycling of polyolefins (PO) via pyrolysis offers a circular pathway for plastic waste management, yet industrial implementation remains hindered by high energy demands and poor product selectivity. Here, we report an Fe-catalyzed pyrolysis process that achieves 97% PO conversion and a 94% yield of C6 to C35 liquid hydrocarbons. By using a zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF)-derived, N-doped porous carbon-supported iron single-atom catalyst (Fe 1 @NC) in combination with a strategic temperature gradient control, we overcome traditional thermolysis limitations. The process was further demonstrated on a kilogram scale, supporting the practical scalability of this catalytic system. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the rate-determining step is an acid base-promoted dehydrogenation of the polymer backbone. Specifically, electronic synergy between the single iron centers and the carbon support stabilizes reactive carbocation intermediates, facilitating their rapid decomposition into high-value olefins and alkanes. These findings provide a scalable and highly efficient catalytic framework for the upcycling of plastic waste into liquid hydrocarbon fractions and chemical feedstocks.
authors: Guo-Ping Lu, Xueping Zhang, Kai Xu, Chenhao Tan, Yamei Lin, Wenbin Yi, Kangkang Sun, Matthias Beller

10.1126/sciadv.aeh1001.title: Adaptive dual-programming magnetic soft robot with lifelike behavior
10.1126/sciadv.aeh1001.abstract: Magnetic soft robots with embodied intelligence of multimodal motions, environmental perception, and functional decoupling depend on ingenious material arrangement and programmable morphing information introduction. While some efforts have been made, achieving lifelike behaviors for soft robots in system-level strategy remains a notable challenge. Here, we present dual-programming hydrogel-based soft robots (DHSRs) that couple magnetic and anisotropic programming through the spatial arrangement of patterned magnetic skeletons into responsive and structural hydrogel bodies. These DHSRs exhibit programmable exquisite and multicurved structures in three-dimensional (3D) space, environment-adaptive deformation behaviors proved by switching from random jumping on land to regular swimming in water of a fish-like soft robot, and further locomotion-function decoupling capabilities of region-selective cargo delivery in an integrated “locomotion-perception-action” workflow. Our strategy in biomedical potential is exemplified by a ring-like pH-responsive DHSR for gastric ulcer therapy, which integrates multimodal locomotion (rolling, tumbling, and rotating), adaptive matching, and microneedle-mediated penetration. By collaborating with a capsule endoscopy system, we explore the possibility of a wireless and painless diagnostic-therapeutic platform in a pig model. This strategy endows the robot with perception and multitask execution capabilities, highlighting a promising route for the intelligent evolution of soft robots across diverse application domains.
authors: Yanchen Ye, Can Xu, Sen Wang, Weijia Li, RongYe Wu, Hao Wu, Neng Xia, TianYe Yang, Shuang Song, Li Zhang, Yue Dong, Bing Li

10.1126/sciadv.aeh1407.title: Age reshapes selection on melanoma driver mutations
10.1126/sciadv.aeh1407.abstract: Aging is a major risk factor for melanoma. However, it is unclear whether aging fuels tumor evolution by altering mutation rates, changing the microenvironmentally induced selection on drivers, or both. We analyzed 5472 melanomas, estimating how selection on individual variants changes with patient age while accounting for differing neutral mutation rates. Neutral mutation rates increased only modestly with age; ultraviolet damage remained predominant, but endogenous processes increasingly contributed to older tumors. In contrast, selection on major drivers was strongly age dependent: The advantage of BRAF V600E declined precipitously with age, whereas NRAS Q61 mutations gained advantage. TERT promoter mutations became more frequent, yet less advantageous. Aging therefore reshapes melanoma evolution primarily by altering selection, motivating age-conscious evaluation of clinical biomarkers and therapies.
authors: Yihan Liu, Jeffrey D. Mandell, Moein Rajaei, Douglas Brash, Jorge Alfaro-Murillo, Jeffrey P. Townsend

10.1126/sciadv.aeh4906.title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
10.1126/sciadv.aeh4906.abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.
authors: Qin-Qin Wang, Xiao-Ye Xu, Yong-Jian Han, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo

10.1126/sciadv.aeh7742.title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
10.1126/sciadv.aeh7742.abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection. The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.
authors: Jikang Xu, Jianlin Wang, Wenjing Liu, Jiaming Zhang, Jingsheng Chen, Xiaobing Yan

10.1126/sciadv.aeh7797.title: Photonic entanglement swapping with remote quantum dots
10.1126/sciadv.aeh7797.abstract: Entanglement swapping is a protocol that details how to create entanglement between previously uncorrelated particles. Its photonic version, mediated by the interference of photon pairs generated by separate quantum systems, finds disparate applications in quantum networks. So far, entanglement swapping with entangled photons from remote systems has been implemented only using probabilistic sources. However, the scaling up of quantum networks requires nonprobabilistic quantum emitters without a trade-off between the degree of entanglement and photon-pair generation rate. Here, we demonstrate photonic entanglement swapping using photon pairs generated by two separate GaAs quantum dots. The emitters are deterministically embedded in hybrid semiconductor-piezoelectric devices that make the entangled photons from two dissimilar quantum dots nearly identical. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated with a fidelity as high as 0.71(2), more than 10 SDs above the classical limit. The experimental data are quantitatively explained by a theoretical model that also suggests how to boost the protocol performance. Our work opens the path to the exploitation of quantum dot entangled-photon sources in quantum repeater networks.

10.1126/sciadv.aeh9111.title: Three-way circulation-soil moisture-temperature feedbacks amplify the most extreme mid-latitudinal heat waves
10.1126/sciadv.aeh9111.abstract: The most extreme heat waves are intensifying faster than moderate events across many mid-latitude regions. Climate models underestimate these trends, suggesting an incomplete representation and understanding of the underlying physical processes. Here, we use an explainable machine-learning framework to investigate interactions among atmospheric circulation, surface soil moisture, and temperature, and their role in recent heat extremes. We show that a three-way interaction among these components becomes active once a critical temperature threshold is exceeded, contributing, on average, ∼10% to peak temperature anomalies during the most extreme heat events across ∼28% of humid mid-latitude regions. We further reveal that this interaction is systematically underestimated in CMIP6 and CESM2 Large Ensemble simulations. Soils in climate models are too dry at the initiation of heat waves, therefore suppressing subsequent soil-moisture depletion and inhibiting feedback activation. These findings help explain regional model biases in upper-tail warming and highlight avenues for improving future projections of extreme heat events.
authors: Yinglin Tian, Jiangong Liu, Yu Huang, Pierre Gentine, Kai Kornhuber

10.1126/sciadv.aei0654.title: Quantum-interference metrology of dissipative Kerr solitons
10.1126/sciadv.aei0654.abstract: Dissipative Kerr solitons in optical microresonators underpin chip-scale frequency combs with applications ranging from coherent telecommunications to precision spectroscopy. Yet the characterization of their intrinsic femtosecond temporal structure remains challenging, as the low pulse energy and broad spectral bandwidth necessitate optical amplification and careful dispersion compensation in conventional ultrafast diagnostics, both of which can substantial distort the waveform. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-interference metrology of microcomb solitons based on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. By attenuating the soliton stream to the single-photon level and measuring fourth-order interference, we directly retrieve near transform-limited pulse durations without amplification or dispersion management, remaining accurate even after propagation through 25 kilometers of standard fiber. The same interferogram also provides direct access to the temporal separations in multisoliton states by converting intersoliton separations into additional interference dips at corresponding delays, enabling subpicosecond characterization of their intracavity temporal structure. This quantum-inspired paradigm introduces a metrological approach that is immune to amplification and dispersion distortions, offering a powerful tool for the characterization of complex soliton physics.
authors: Yun-Ru Fan, Yong Geng, Ji Liu, Yong-Jun Huang, Hai-Zhi Song, Hao Li, Li-Xing You, Heng Zhou, Kun Qiu, Kai Guo, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou

10.1126/sciadv.aei4524.title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery
10.1126/sciadv.aei4524.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli -infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.
authors: Dwaipayan Basu, Yajie Gu, Ying-Xing Li, Taylor Forman, Majid Ghassemian, Ryan K. Min, Joe Pogliano, Kevin D. Corbett

10.1126/sciadv.aei8257.title: High-impulse and reactant-regenerative combustion-based micro actuators
10.1126/sciadv.aei8257.abstract: The use of combustibles in micro-actuator technologies enables powerful impulsive actuation capabilities comparable to those of natural organisms. However, the exogenous dependence of fuel limits the development of combustion-based actuators. We present a closed-cycle reactant regeneration strategy wherein the bidirectional interconversion between hydrogen and water achieves real-time fuel replenishment for reactant-regenerative electrolysis and combustion reactions. Based on this, we develop a 1.5-centimeter actuator that generates forces above 20 newtons and operates continuously for >7200 cycles without refueling (a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over existing combustion-based actuators). Experiments confirm its strength and cross-environment versatility for removing obstacles, jetting, and striking via underwater cavitation. These features enable the actuator to be integrated into small robotic platforms, allowing them to reconfigure local surroundings in an active manner.
authors: Jihong Yin, Dongkai Wang, Dazhe Zhao, Yanting Gong, Junwen Zhong

10.1126/sciadv.aei8633.title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
10.1126/sciadv.aei8633.abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.
authors: Charley Mackenzie-Kludas, Wen-Yang Wu, Betty Jin, Jennifer L. McKimm-Breschkin, Ee Ling Seah, Paul Jones, Emily Fairmaid, Celeste M. K. Tai, Ding Yuan Oh, Peter J. Jenkins, Aeron C. Hurt, Lorena E. Brown

10.1126/sciadv.aej2234.title: Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
10.1126/sciadv.aej2234.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.
authors: Haiyang Yu, Meng Zhang, Yihang Zhang, Jindong Li, Liu Yang, Yuehua Wang, Li Chen, Ruifeng Yao

10.1126/sciadv.aej2662.title: MYC primes a paralog synthetic lethality involving the mitochondrial translocase subunits TIMM17A and TIMM17B and N-Acetylaspartate
10.1126/sciadv.aej2662.abstract: To identify the genes and pathways required for the survival of MYC -amplified cancers, we engineered an isogenic cell system in which transformation is driven by oncogenic MYC . Using a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 library, we identified the mitochondrial membrane translocase TIMM17A as uniquely essential for the survival of MYC-transformed cells. This dependency arises from MYC-driven suppression of TIMM17B , the paralog of TIMM17A . TIMM17A/B is an essential component of the TIM23 mitochondrial protein import complex, and the MYC-induced suppression of TIMM17B creates a strong dependency on TIMM17A . N-acetylaspartate supplementation rescued TIMM17A dependency in MYC -amplified cell lines, highlighting the unique and crucial role of this metabolite in the cell fitness of MYC -amplified cancers. These observations identify a paralog dependency required for the survival of a subset of MYC-driven cancers.

10.1126/sciadv.aej4381.title: CD8+ T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
10.1126/sciadv.aej4381.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)-regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell-dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell-mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell-induced endothelial death in CM.

10.1126/sciadv.aej6039.title: Molecular engineering of noncoordinating backbones in Zr-MOFs for ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism-based high pressure sensing
10.1126/sciadv.aej6039.abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising pressure-responsive luminescent materials, but precise control of their emission under pressure remains a substantial challenge. Here, we engineered the piezofluorochromic response of zirconium-based MOFs by tuning the polarity of the emissive moieties through noncoordinating phenyl substituents. Four isostructural UiO-67 derivatives were synthesized. The most polar ligand, in UiO-67-PA, yields ultrasensitive piezofluorochromism with a bathochromic shift of 190 nanometers per gigapascal below 0.36 gigapascals. This sensitivity arises from two cooperative effects: enhanced conjugation through pressure-driven rotation of the aromatic rings and amplified orbital overlap resulting from polarity-induced electronic redistribution. This work broadens the strategies for modulating MOF luminescence and highlights their potential for pressure sensing.
authors: Pengxiang Dong, Cha Li, Shiwei Yao, Xin-Ping Gao, Feifan Lang, Kai Wang, Fangna Dai, Jiandong Pang, Xian-He Bu

10.1126/sciadv.aek2522.title: A single-amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking
10.1126/sciadv.aek2522.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.
